papers.title: Microscopic and collective signatures of feature learning in neural networks
papers.research_question: What are the collective and microscopic signatures of feature learning in Bayesian shallow neural networks in the proportional regime?
papers.core_contribution: In the proportional regime, feature learning in Bayesian shallow neural networks is characterized by a nonmonotonic distance between class manifolds and finite, data-dependent weight correlations.
papers.conclusion: The squared distance between class manifolds and the finite weight correlations are collective and microscopic signatures of feature learning in Bayesian shallow networks in the proportional regime.
papers.key_findings:
The posterior distance between class manifolds remains unaltered in the infinite-width limit but departs from its prior value at proportional width.
The average squared distance is a nonmonotonic function of temperature, and this nonmonotonicity disappears in the infinite-width limit or when labels are randomized.
The hidden-layer weights become correlated in the proportional regime, undergoing a finite displacement.
The nonmonotonicity of the distance aligns with inversion dynamics observed during gradient descent training, serving as an equilibrium counterpart.
The second-order statistics of the weights depends on input patterns in a way not traceable to the infinite-width limit.
papers.limitation:
The results are limited to standard-scaled neural networks and do not apply to mean-field scaling.
The theory does not characterize feature learning closer to the interpolation threshold.
papers.abstract: Feature extraction - the ability to identify relevant properties of data - is a key factor underlying the success of deep learning. Yet, it has proved difficult to elucidate its nature within existing predictive theories, to the extent that there is no consensus on the very definition of feature learning. A promising hint in this direction comes from previous phenomenological observations of quasi-universal aspects in the training dynamics of neural networks, displayed by simple properties of feature geometry. We address this problem within a statistical-mechanics framework for Bayesian learning in one hidden layer neural networks with standard parameterization. Analytical computations in the proportional limit (when both the network width and the size of the training set are large) can quantify fingerprints of feature learning, both collective ones (related to manifold geometry) and microscopic ones (related to the weights). In particular, (i) the distance between different class manifolds in feature space is a nonmonotonic function of the temperature, which we interpret as the equilibrium counterpart of a phenomenon observed under gradient descent (GD) dynamics, and (ii) the microscopic learnable parameters in the network undergo a finite data-dependent displacement with respect to the infinite-width limit, and develop correlations. These results indicate that nontrivial feature learning is at play in a regime where the posterior predictive distribution is that of Gaussian process regression with a trivially rescaled prior.

papers.title: Transformers learn factored representations
papers.research_question: Do transformers learn to factor their world into parts from next-token prediction, and why would they have an inductive bias for factored representations?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers learn to factor their world into parts, representing each factor in orthogonal subspaces of the residual stream, and show an inductive bias toward factored representations even when it is lossy.
papers.conclusion: Transformers decompose the world into parts and represent them in orthogonal subspaces due to an inductive bias from next-token prediction, suggesting interpretable low-dimensional structure may persist in models trained on complex data.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers learn factored representations in orthogonal subspaces when data has conditionally independent factors.
The dimensionality of activations collapses to the linearly growing factored prediction, not the exponentially growing joint representation.
Factor subspaces become approximately orthogonal over training, as measured by subspace overlap and dimensionality additivity.
Factoring begins at the token embedding layer, with the embedding matrix developing low-rank structure corresponding to factor subspaces.
Transformers exhibit an inductive bias toward factored representations, learning them early even when data is not perfectly factorable, sacrificing fidelity for dimensional efficiency.
papers.limitation: Experiments are conducted on synthetic data with known latent structure, which may not fully capture real-world complexity.
future_direction: Investigate whether differences in factorization behavior between transformers, RNNs, and LSTMs are due to training dynamics or inductive bias.
papers.abstract: Transformers pretrained via next token prediction learn to factor their world into parts, representing these factors in orthogonal subspaces of the residual stream. We formalize two representational hypotheses: (1) a representation in the product space of all factors, whose dimension grows exponentially with the number of parts, or (2) a factored representation in orthogonal subspaces, whose dimension grows linearly. The factored representation is lossless when factors are conditionally independent, but sacrifices predictive fidelity otherwise, creating a tradeoff between dimensional efficiency and accuracy. We derive precise predictions about the geometric structure of activations for each, including the number of subspaces, their dimensionality, and the arrangement of context embeddings within them. We test between these hypotheses on transformers trained on synthetic processes with known latent structure. Models learn factored representations when factors are conditionally independent, and continue to favor them early in training even when noise or hidden dependencies undermine conditional independence, reflecting an inductive bias toward factoring at the cost of fidelity. This provides a principled explanation for why transformers decompose the world into parts, and suggests that interpretable low dimensional structure may persist even in models trained on complex data.

papers.title: Interpreting Equivariant Representations
papers.research_question: How can we properly interpret equivariant latent representations, and how can we obtain invariant representations from equivariant models to avoid misleading conclusions and improve downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the importance of considering the inductive bias of equivariant models when interpreting latent representations and provides principles for choosing invariant projections to obtain unambiguous and informative invariant representations, which improve downstream analysis.
papers.conclusion: Invariant projections are essential for the proper interpretation and utilization of equivariant latent representations, and the proposed tools—isometric cross sections and random invariant projections—effectively address the inherent ambiguity, leading to more reliable downstream analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Equivariant latent representations are ambiguous because each input maps to a set of latent vectors (an orbit) under the group action, leading to ill-defined distances and potentially misleading visualizations and analyses.
Invariant projections, such as sorting for permutation-equivariant representations or random invariant linear projections for rotation-equivariant representations, can extract invariant features that preserve information and improve downstream task performance.
For permutation-equivariant VAEs, an isometric invariant representation obtained by sorting the latent coordinates forms a convex cone, enabling meaningful linear interpolation between molecules.
For rotation-equivariant classifiers, random invariant projections retain a high degree of information and yield latent spaces with clear structure, improving visualization and kNN classification accuracy.
The ambiguity observed in strictly equivariant models also appears in standard deep learning models where invariance is encouraged via data augmentation, highlighting the broader relevance of the issue.
papers.limitation: Choosing a suitable invariant mapping may not always be clear and can depend greatly on the model architecture.
future_direction: Suggesting suitable high-quality invariant mappings relevant for widely applied equivariant architectures.
papers.abstract: Latent representations are used extensively for downstream tasks, such as visualization, interpolation or feature extraction of deep learning models. Invariant and equivariant neural networks are powerful and well-established models for enforcing inductive biases. In this paper, we demonstrate that the inductive bias imposed on the by an equivariant model must also be taken into account when using latent representations. We show how not accounting for the inductive biases leads to decreased performance on downstream tasks, and vice versa, how accounting for inductive biases can be done effectively by using an invariant projection of the latent representations. We propose principles for how to choose such a projection, and show the impact of using these principles in two common examples: First, we study a permutation equivariant variational auto-encoder trained for molecule graph generation; here we show that invariant projections can be designed that incur no loss of information in the resulting invariant representation. Next, we study a rotation-equivariant representation used for image classification. Here, we illustrate how random invariant projections can be used to obtain an invariant representation with a high degree of retained information. In both cases, the analysis of invariant latent representations proves superior to their equivariant counterparts. Finally, we illustrate that the phenomena documented here for equivariant neural networks have counterparts in standard neural networks where invariance is encouraged via augmentation. Thus, while these ambiguities may be known by experienced developers of equivariant models, we make both the knowledge as well as effective tools to handle the ambiguities available to the broader community.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
papers.abstract: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior. The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: Convolutional neural networks can identify brain interactions involved in decoding spatial auditory attention
papers.research_question: Can a convolutional neural network (CNN) be designed to learn task-specific interactions between brain regions from source-reconstructed EEG data to decode spatial auditory attention, rather than being used as a black box decoder?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretable CNN architecture that learns pairwise interactions between brain regions from source-reconstructed EEG data to decode spatial auditory attention, and demonstrates that this model identifies known important neural interactions and frequency bands.
papers.conclusion: The CNN model can effectively utilize features known to be important in auditory attention tasks, suggesting that domain knowledge-inspired CNNs applied to source-reconstructed EEG data offer a novel computational framework for studying task-relevant brain interactions.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN model achieved median decoding accuracies of 77.56% (within-participant) and 65.14% (cross-participant) for spatial auditory attention.
Analysis of the model's spatial filters revealed alpha-band-dominated inter-hemisphere interactions and alpha- and beta-band dominant interactions that were hemisphere-specific or showed contrasting patterns between hemispheres.
These interactions were more pronounced in parietal and central regions for within-participant decoding, and in parietal, central, and partly frontal regions for cross-participant decoding.
Ablation analysis showed that parietal, temporal, and central brain regions are important for decoding performance.
Removing alpha and beta frequency bands from the input data significantly decreased model performance, indicating their key role.
papers.limitation:
The CNN architecture may not be deep enough to capture longer temporal structures (e.g., delta and theta frequencies), and increasing depth could lead to overfitting due to limited data.
Decoding performance varied across participants, which may be related to the relatively low number of trials per participant and the small overall number of participants.
The use of 64-channel EEG for source reconstruction may yield less precise localization compared to high-density EEG or MEG systems.
future_direction: Future research may use more data, employ data augmentation techniques, utilize more flexible CNN architectures, and/or include behavioral data to account for inter-individual heterogeneity.
Future studies may explore other architectures to adapt the model to brain dynamics, such as incorporating attention layers or graph convolutional neural networks.
Future work could develop a CNN model that integrates both stimulus information (e.g., speech envelopes) and EEG signals to decode auditory attention and study entrainment mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Human listeners have the ability to direct their attention to a single speaker in a multi-talker environment. The neural correlates of selective attention can be decoded from a single trial of electroencephalography (EEG) data. In this study, leveraging the source-reconstructed and anatomically-resolved EEG data as inputs, we sought to employ CNN as an interpretable model to uncover task-specific interactions between brain regions, rather than simply to utilize it as a black box decoder. To this end, our CNN model was specifically designed to learn pairwise interaction representations for 10 cortical regions from five-second inputs. By exclusively utilizing these features for decoding, our model was able to attain a median accuracy of 77.56% for within-participant and 65.14% for cross-participant classification. Through ablation analysis together with dissecting the features of the models and applying cluster analysis, we were able to discern the presence of alpha-band-dominated inter-hemisphere interactions, as well as alpha- and beta-band dominant interactions that were either hemisphere-specific or were characterized by a contrasting pattern between the right and left hemispheres. These interactions were more pronounced in parietal and central regions for within-participant decoding, but in parietal, central, and partly frontal regions for cross-participant decoding. These findings demonstrate that our CNN model can effectively utilize features known to be important in auditory attention tasks and suggest that the application of domain knowledge inspired CNNs on source-reconstructed EEG data can offer a novel computational framework for studying task-relevant brain interactions.

papers.title: Getting a CLUE: A Method for Explaining Uncertainty Estimates
papers.research_question: What input patterns are responsible for predictive uncertainty in probabilistic models, and how can we generate counterfactual explanations to reduce uncertainty while keeping inputs on the data manifold?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Counterfactual Latent Uncertainty Explanations (CLUE), a method that generates counterfactual explanations for uncertainty estimates by optimizing in the latent space of a deep generative model, and proposes a computational framework for evaluating such explanations.
papers.conclusion: CLUE is an effective method for explaining uncertainty estimates, providing actionable insights for practitioners to understand which input patterns are responsible for predictive uncertainty.
papers.key_findings:
CLUE outperforms baseline methods (Localized Sensitivity and U-FIDO) in explaining uncertainty across multiple datasets.
CLUE generates counterfactuals that are both informative (reduce uncertainty) and relevant (stay on the data manifold).
The proposed computational evaluation framework effectively measures the trade-off between informativeness and relevance.
User studies show that CLUE helps practitioners better identify sources of uncertainty compared to baselines.
CLUE is effective for both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty, and for both tabular and image data.
papers.limitation: CLUE's performance depends on the quality of the auxiliary deep generative model; if the DGM does not capture the data manifold well, CLUE may generate unrealistic counterfactuals.
future_direction: Extending CLUE to other probabilistic models beyond BNNs
Applying CLUE in active learning and Bayesian optimization scenarios
papers.abstract: Both uncertainty estimation and interpretability are important factors for trustworthy machine learning systems. However, there is little work at the intersection of these two areas. We address this gap by proposing a novel method for interpreting uncertainty estimates from differentiable probabilistic models, like Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). Our method, Counterfactual Latent Uncertainty Explanations (CLUE), indicates how to change an input, while keeping it on the data manifold, such that a BNN becomes more confident about the input's prediction. We validate CLUE through 1) a novel framework for evaluating counterfactual explanations of uncertainty, 2) a series of ablation experiments, and 3) a user study. Our experiments show that CLUE outperforms baselines and enables practitioners to better understand which input patterns are responsible for predictive uncertainty.

papers.title: What shapes feature representations? Exploring datasets, architectures, and training
papers.research_question: What features do models use and represent when there are multiple task-relevant or irrelevant features, and how do inductive biases and training affect this?
papers.core_contribution: Models preferentially represent features that are more decodable from the untrained model, enhancing task-relevant features and suppressing irrelevant ones, and sometimes suppress more predictive but harder features in favor of easier ones.
papers.conclusion: Model representations are shaped by inductive biases and training; practitioners should not assume label-relevant features are used; analyzing untrained models can predict feature usage; representational similarity analyses should be interpreted with care.
papers.key_findings:
Many input features are partially represented in untrained models.
Training enhances task-relevant features and suppresses task-irrelevant features.
When two features redundantly predict the label, models prefer the one more decodable from the untrained model.
An easier, weakly predictive feature can suppress a more strongly predictive but harder feature.
Easy features lead to more consistent representations across model runs than hard features, and multi-task models resemble those trained only on the easy feature.
papers.limitation: The results are shown across multiple architectures and datasets but may not generalize to broader settings.
future_direction: Explore broader settings beyond the architectures and datasets studied.
Investigate the effect of fully-connected layer width on feature representations.
papers.abstract: In naturalistic learning problems, a model's input contains a wide range of features, some useful for the task at hand, and others not. Of the useful features, which ones does the model use? Of the task-irrelevant features, which ones does the model represent? Answers to these questions are important for understanding the basis of models' decisions, as well as for building models that learn versatile, adaptable representations useful beyond the original training task. We study these questions using synthetic datasets in which the task-relevance of input features can be controlled directly. We find that when two features redundantly predict the labels, the model preferentially represents one, and its preference reflects what was most linearly decodable from the untrained model. Over training, task-relevant features are enhanced, and task-irrelevant features are partially suppressed. Interestingly, in some cases, an easier, weakly predictive feature can suppress a more strongly predictive, but more difficult one. Additionally, models trained to recognize both easy and hard features learn representations most similar to models that use only the easy feature. Further, easy features lead to more consistent representations across model runs than do hard features. Finally, models have greater representational similarity to an untrained model than to models trained on a different task. Our results highlight the complex processes that determine which features a model represents.

papers.title: Large Language Models Encode Semantics and Alignment in Linearly Separable Representations
papers.research_question: To what extent do large language models encode high-level semantic information in linearly separable representations across domains and alignment behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode high-level semantics and alignment behaviors in linearly separable representations, enabling effective latent-space guardrails for safety.
papers.conclusion: LLMs organize high-level semantics and alignment in linearly separable subspaces, motivating geometry-aware tools for safer deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic representations become increasingly linearly separable in deeper layers.
Linear separability persists even when domain-specific keywords are masked.
Instruction following (e.g., chain-of-thought) induces linearly separable representations.
Safety-aligned models show separable clusters for benign and harmful prompts.
A lightweight MLP guardrail on hidden states improves refusal rates on adversarial prompts.
future_direction: Adversarial perturbation studies for causal validation
Axis-orthogonality tests for linear representations
Further research on information distribution across architectures
papers.abstract: Understanding the latent space geometry of large language models (LLMs) is key to interpreting their behavior and improving alignment. Yet it remains unclear to what extent LLMs linearly organize representations related to semantic understanding. To explore this, we conduct a large-scale empirical study of hidden representations in 11 autoregressive models across six scientific topics. We find that high-level semantic information consistently resides in low-dimensional subspaces that form linearly separable representations across domains. This separability becomes more pronounced in deeper layers and under prompts that elicit structured reasoning or alignment behavior$\unicode{x2013}$even when surface content remains unchanged. These findings motivate geometry-aware tools that operate directly in latent space to detect and mitigate harmful and adversarial content. As a proof of concept, we train an MLP probe on final-layer hidden states as a lightweight latent-space guardrail. This approach substantially improves refusal rates on malicious queries and prompt injections that bypass both the model's built-in safety alignment and external token-level filters.

papers.title: ProtoVAE: A Trustworthy Self-Explainable Prototypical Variational Model
papers.research_question: How to build a self-explainable model that is transparent, diverse, and trustworthy without sacrificing predictive performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ProtoV AE, a variational autoencoder-based self-explainable model that learns class-specific prototypes end-to-end, enforces diversity and trustworthiness via regularization, and achieves predictive performance comparable to black-box models.
papers.conclusion: ProtoV AE satisfies the defined properties of transparency, diversity, and trustworthiness for self-explainable models, providing faithful explanations without degrading predictive performance.
papers.key_findings:
ProtoV AE achieves better predictive accuracy than other self-explainable models and matches or exceeds black-box model performance.
The model learns diverse and transparent prototypes that can be visualized in the input space via the decoder.
Local explanation maps generated via Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) are more faithful than those of ProtoPNet.
The orthonormality constraint and VAE loss prevent prototype collapse and ensure intra-class diversity.
ProtoV AE's prototypes represent the 'true mean' of data subsets, providing more flexible and faithful global explanations.
papers.limitation:
The number of prototypes per class is fixed, which may not adapt to classes of varying complexity.
The quality of global explanations (prototype reconstructions) is limited by the decoder's capability.
future_direction: Distance-based pruning of prototypes to adapt their number per class.
Using a prior on the distribution of prototypical similarities to control prototype usage frequency.
Leveraging more expressive generative models (e.g., very deep VAEs, normalizing flows) to improve prototype reconstructions and scalability.
papers.abstract: The need for interpretable models has fostered the development of self-explainable classifiers. Prior approaches are either based on multi-stage optimization schemes, impacting the predictive performance of the model, or produce explanations that are not transparent, trustworthy or do not capture the diversity of the data. To address these shortcomings, we propose ProtoVAE, a variational autoencoder-based framework that learns class-specific prototypes in an end-to-end manner and enforces trustworthiness and diversity by regularizing the representation space and introducing an orthonormality constraint. Finally, the model is designed to be transparent by directly incorporating the prototypes into the decision process. Extensive comparisons with previous self-explainable approaches demonstrate the superiority of ProtoVAE, highlighting its ability to generate trustworthy and diverse explanations, while not degrading predictive performance.

papers.title: Understanding Generative AI Content with Embedding Models
papers.research_question: Can embedding vectors from foundation models reveal semantic distinctions in data, particularly separability between real and AI-generated samples?
papers.core_contribution: Embedding vectors from foundation models, when combined with dimensionality reduction, can separate real and AI-generated data, revealing inherent biases (generative DNA) in generative models.
papers.conclusion: Feature embedders can reveal statistical biases in generative models and provide a foundation for automated detection of AI-generated content.
papers.key_findings:
Embedding vectors from feature embedders (FEs) can separate data from different sources, including real vs. AI-generated.
The separability is due to differences in sampling techniques and generative model biases (generative DNA).
Even after normalization (e.g., translation), differences persist due to content and style.
Simple classifiers like Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) achieve high accuracy in distinguishing real and AI-generated data.
The signal in embedded data is low-dimensional, explaining why distributional shifts are easily detectable.
papers.limitation: For short text samples (e.g., one sentence), it is difficult to distinguish between human and machine translations.
papers.abstract: Constructing high-quality features is critical to any quantitative data analysis. While feature engineering was historically addressed by carefully hand-crafting data representations based on domain expertise, deep neural networks (DNNs) now offer a radically different approach. DNNs implicitly engineer features by transforming their input data into hidden feature vectors called embeddings. For embedding vectors produced by foundation models -- which are trained to be useful across many contexts -- we demonstrate that simple and well-studied dimensionality-reduction techniques such as Principal Component Analysis uncover inherent heterogeneity in input data concordant with human-understandable explanations. Of the many applications for this framework, we find empirical evidence that there is intrinsic separability between real samples and those generated by artificial intelligence (AI).

papers.title: Evaluation of CNN Performance in Semantically Relevant Latent Spaces
papers.research_question: How can we validate and explain CNN predictions by using a semantically relevant latent space to generate contrastive explanations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a framework that uses a weakly-supervised variational autoencoder (VAE) with metric learning to create a semantically relevant latent space, which is then used to validate CNN predictions via a linear SVM and generate contrastive explanations by traversing the latent space.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework allows for the validation and explanation of CNN predictions by utilizing a semantically relevant latent space, enabling the generation of contrastive explanations to answer 'why a and not b?' questions.
papers.key_findings:
The triplet-VAE creates a better separated and semantically relevant latent space compared to a vanilla VAE, as shown by t-SNE visualizations and improved linear separability.
The framework can identify cases where the CNN and SVM predictions disagree, allowing for further investigation.
The method can generate contrastive explanations by showing the minimal semantic changes needed in an input image to change the CNN's prediction to another class.
papers.limitation: The framework cannot detect cases where both the CNN and SVM agree on a prediction that is incorrect (case 2 in Table 1) without generating explanations for every decision.
papers.abstract: We examine deep neural network (DNN) performance and behavior using contrasting explanations generated from a semantically relevant latent space. We develop a semantically relevant latent space by training a variational autoencoder (VAE) augmented by a metric learning loss on the latent space. The properties of the VAE provide for a smooth latent space supported by a simple density and the metric learning term organizes the space in a semantically relevant way with respect to the target classes. In this space we can both linearly separate the classes and generate meaningful interpolation of contrasting data points across decision boundaries. This allows us to examine the DNN model beyond its performance on a test set for potential biases and its sensitivity to perturbations of individual factors disentangled in the latent space.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: Variational Classification
papers.research_question: What is the probabilistic interpretation of neural network softmax classifiers? How can we generalize softmax classification to align the empirical latent distribution with the anticipated latent distribution to improve properties like calibration, robustness, and sample efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Variational Classification (VC), a latent variable model that generalizes softmax classification, providing theoretical insight and improving calibration, adversarial robustness, robustness to distribution shift, and sample efficiency without extra hyperparameters.
papers.conclusion: Variational Classification generalizes softmax classification from a latent perspective, provides new theoretical insight, and empirically improves multiple desirable properties of classifiers without additional hyperparameters.
papers.key_findings:
VC maintains classification accuracy comparable to standard softmax classifiers.
VC significantly improves calibration (lower ECE) across multiple datasets and architectures.
VC enhances robustness to distribution shift, both synthetic and natural, as measured by calibration error.
VC increases adversarial robustness against FGSM attacks.
VC improves performance in low-data regimes, with benefits increasing as training samples decrease.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on the output layer of a classifier, treating the encoder as a black-box.
Optimal empirical latent distributions are peaky approximations to the anticipated distributions, leaving room for further improvement.
future_direction: Extend q(z|x) to a stochastic distribution rather than a delta distribution.
Apply VC to semi-supervised learning.
Relate VC to approaches that impose structure in the latent space.
papers.abstract: We present a latent variable model for classification that provides a novel probabilistic interpretation of neural network softmax classifiers. We derive a variational objective to train the model, analogous to the evidence lower bound (ELBO) used to train variational auto-encoders, that generalises the softmax cross-entropy loss. Treating inputs to the softmax layer as samples of a latent variable, our abstracted perspective reveals a potential inconsistency between their anticipated distribution, required for accurate label predictions, and their empirical distribution found in practice. We augment the variational objective to mitigate such inconsistency and induce a chosen latent distribution, instead of the implicit assumption found in a standard softmax layer. Overall, we provide new theoretical insight into the inner workings of widely-used softmax classifiers. Empirical evaluation on image and text classification datasets demonstrates that our proposed approach, variational classification, maintains classification accuracy while the reshaped latent space improves other desirable properties of a classifier, such as calibration, adversarial robustness, robustness to distribution shift and sample efficiency useful in low data settings.

papers.title: Latent space configuration for improved generalization in supervised autoencoder neural networks
papers.research_question: How can the properties and topology of a supervised autoencoder's latent space be directly controlled to improve generalization and enable new capabilities like similarity estimation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes two methods (loss configuration via a geometric loss term and encoder configuration) to directly control the topology of a supervised autoencoder's latent space, leading to more stable training, improved generalization, and enabling similarity estimation and text-based search without classifiers or language models.
papers.conclusion: Latent space configuration via geometric loss or encoder modification allows control over latent space topology, leading to more stable and interpretable training, improved generalization, and new capabilities for similarity estimation and text-based search without additional models.
papers.key_findings:
Training with the proposed geometric loss reliably produces a latent space with a predetermined, stable cluster configuration, unlike conventional training which yields unpredictable and varied latent space distributions.
The method improves generalization accuracy, as shown by texture classification tasks on unseen data from LIP, Market1501, and WildTrack datasets without fine-tuning.
The known latent space configuration allows the definition of a similarity measure to compare inputs directly in latent space, enabling image retrieval and similarity ranking without using the classifier.
The method enables cross-dataset searches (e.g., query from Market1501 searched in WildTrack) and text-query-based searches without the need for a separate language model by correlating text descriptions with known latent space regions.
Encoder configuration (e.g., using polar coordinates) guarantees the desired latent space properties during inference but is more invasive and presents training difficulties.
papers.limitation: Test accuracy is not very high, partly due to the small dataset size and inherent visual similarity between certain texture classes (e.g., folds on uniform texture misclassified as lines, low-resolution patterns becoming indistinguishable).
future_direction: Extending the geometric loss formulation and encoder configuration methods to n-dimensional latent spaces and non-Euclidean topologies (e.g., hyperbolic spaces).

Applying the latent space configuration methodology to generative models like diffusion models, though the means of doing so with high-dimensional latent spaces (e.g., 4096) are not obvious and require future study.
papers.abstract: Autoencoders (AE) are simple yet powerful class of neural networks that compress data by projecting input into low-dimensional latent space (LS). Whereas LS is formed according to the loss function minimization during training, its properties and topology are not controlled directly. In this paper we focus on AE LS properties and propose two methods for obtaining LS with desired topology, called LS configuration. The proposed methods include loss configuration using a geometric loss term that acts directly in LS, and encoder configuration. We show that the former allows to reliably obtain LS with desired configuration by defining the positions and shapes of LS clusters for supervised AE (SAE). Knowing LS configuration allows to define similarity measure in LS to predict labels or estimate similarity for multiple inputs without using decoders or classifiers. We also show that this leads to more stable and interpretable training. We show that SAE trained for clothes texture classification using the proposed method generalizes well to unseen data from LIP, Market1501, and WildTrack datasets without fine-tuning, and even allows to evaluate similarity for unseen classes. We further illustrate the advantages of pre-configured LS similarity estimation with cross-dataset searches and text-based search using a text query without language models.

papers.title: Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations of Bayesian Predictive Models via Kullback-Leibler Projections
papers.research_question: How to explain predictions of Bayesian predictive models by locally projecting the predictive distribution to a simpler, interpretable model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces KL-LIME, a method for local interpretable explanations of Bayesian predictive models by projecting the predictive distribution to a simpler model via KL divergence, accounting for model uncertainty.
papers.conclusion: KL-LIME extends LIME to Bayesian models and provides a principled way to handle different types of predictions and account for model uncertainty in explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The method provides a principled way to explain Bayesian models by projecting the predictive distribution to a simpler interpretable model.
The relative explanatory power curve helps navigate the trade-off between explanation fidelity and complexity.
The method can reveal which parts of an input (e.g., pixels) contribute to a classification decision and the uncertainty in the explanation.
papers.abstract: We introduce a method, KL-LIME, for explaining predictions of Bayesian predictive models by projecting the information in the predictive distribution locally to a simpler, interpretable explanation model. The proposed approach combines the recent Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) method with ideas from Bayesian projection predictive variable selection methods. The information theoretic basis helps in navigating the trade-off between explanation fidelity and complexity. We demonstrate the method in explaining MNIST digit classifications made by a Bayesian deep convolutional neural network.

papers.title: Compressing and interpreting word embeddings with latent space regularization and interactive semantics probing
papers.research_question: How to compress and regularize high-dimensional word embeddings into a lower-dimensional latent space while preserving semantic information and making the latent dimensions more interpretable?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces using β-VAE to compress and regularize word embeddings into a lower-dimensional latent space, making latent dimensions more semantically salient, and provides a visual analytics system for interactive semantics probing.
papers.conclusion: β-VAE effectively compresses and regularizes word embeddings, and the visual analytics system aids in interpreting the latent dimensions, making the embeddings more interpretable and efficient.
papers.key_findings:
β-VAE compresses embeddings by deprecating some latent dimensions, with the remaining dimensions being more semantically salient.
The compressed embeddings from β-VAE perform comparably to the original embeddings in downstream tasks like semantic similarity and word translation.
The visual analytics system effectively helps interpret the latent dimensions and the regularization process.
papers.limitation:
Relies on the linear assumption of semantics in the high-dimensional latent space.
Lacks informative hints to guide users in exploring a large number of latent dimensions.
No rigorous evaluation with users of different backgrounds and expertise.
future_direction: Explore more VAE architectures and other ways to regularize the latent space.
Incorporate human supervision to guide the training for specific semantics.
Study how to perturb multiple latent dimensions concurrently and develop a visual interface for such interactions.
papers.abstract: Word embedding, a high-dimensional (HD) numerical representation of words generated by machine learning models, has been used for different natural language processing tasks, for example, translation between two languages. Recently, there has been an increasing trend of transforming the HD embeddings into a latent space (e.g. via autoencoders) for further tasks, exploiting various merits the latent representations could bring. To preserve the embeddings’ quality, these works often map the embeddings into an even higher-dimensional latent space, making the already complicated embeddings even less interpretable and consuming more storage space. In this work, we borrow the idea of [Formula: see text] VAE to regularize the HD latent space. Our regularization implicitly condenses information from the HD latent space into a much lower-dimensional space, thus compressing the embeddings. We also show that each dimension of our regularized latent space is more semantically salient, and validate our assertion by interactively probing the encoding-level of user-proposed semantics in the dimensions. To the end, we design a visual analytics system to monitor the regularization process, explore the HD latent space, and interpret latent dimensions’ semantics. We validate the effectiveness of our embedding regularization and interpretation approach through both quantitative and qualitative evaluations.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Interpretable Structure in Small Gene Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders extract biologically meaningful representations from small gene language models?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract biologically meaningful representations from small gene language models, revealing features like nucleotide identity and transcription factor binding motifs, demonstrating that compact models learn structured genomic representations.
papers.conclusion: SAEs can extract biologically meaningful representations from small gene language models, highlighting their ability to capture essential genomic features.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs extracted sparse features corresponding to individual nucleotides with high precision.
SAEs identified features aligned with known transcription factor binding motifs, such as MA1596.1 and MA0052.5.
Even compact models effectively capture transcription factor binding specificity.
The recall variability indicates the complexity and redundancy of regulatory elements in genomic sequences.
future_direction: Extend SAE approach to other genomic contexts like non-coding regions or species-specific variations.
Explore SAEs for model refinement and interpretability across different architectures.
Apply SAEs to other biological modalities like single-cell gene expression and multi-omics datasets.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a powerful tool for interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs), revealing latent latent features with semantical meaning. This interpretability has also proven valuable in biological domains: applying SAEs to protein language models uncovered meaningful features related to protein structure and function. More recently, SAEs have been used to analyze genomics-focused models such as Evo 2, identifying interpretable features in gene sequences. However, it remains unclear whether SAEs can extract meaningful representations from small gene language models, which have fewer parameters and potentially less expressive capacity. To address it, we propose applying SAEs to the activations of a small gene language model. We demonstrate that even small-scale models encode biologically relevant genomic features, such as transcription factor binding motifs, that SAEs can effectively uncover. Our findings suggest that compact gene language models are capable of learning structured genomic representations, and that SAEs offer a scalable approach for interpreting gene models across various model sizes.

papers.title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Energy Models: Fast, Interpretable Generative Modeling
papers.research_question: How can we design latent priors for generative models that are efficient, stable, interpretable, and can incorporate domain knowledge, bridging the trade-off between simple priors and costly iterative samplers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Kolmogorov-Arnold Energy Model (KAEM), a generative model that uses a univariate latent structure based on the Kolmogorov-Arnold Representation Theorem to enable fast, exact inference via inverse transform sampling and offers interpretability of the learned prior.
papers.conclusion: KAEM is a promising step towards interpretable generative models that combine fast inference, competitive sample quality, and the potential for incorporating structural inductive biases, laying groundwork for further exploration of the Kolmogorov-Arnold Representation Theorem in machine learning.
papers.key_findings:
KAEM enables fast and exact inference via inverse transform sampling, avoiding costly Markov chain Monte Carlo methods.
Importance sampling becomes a viable and efficient training strategy for simple datasets due to the low-dimensional latent space.
For complex datasets, a population-based sampling strategy using thermodynamic integration and power posteriors improves mixing and exploration.
KAEM generates samples of competitive quality compared to VAEs on SVHN and CelebA datasets.
The learned univariate priors are interpretable and can be visualized, offering a path for latent discovery and knowledge transfer.
papers.limitation:
Training with Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (ULA) does not scale efficiently on GPUs due to its iterative, gradient-based nature and irregular memory access patterns.
Importance sampling fails on complex datasets (e.g., SVHN, CelebA) due to prior-posterior mismatch, necessitating the use of ULA.
The search operations required for inverse transform sampling and residual resampling are difficult to parallelize on GPUs, leading to suboptimal performance.
future_direction: Utilizing the XPU, a reconfigurable dataflow accelerator, for more efficient implementation of KAEM's univariate structure and sampling operations.
Expanding the role of importance sampling by learning in a reduced-order space (e.g., via PCA) or incorporating domain knowledge to shape the prior.
Improving expressivity by exploring different KAN bases, mixture-of-experts frameworks, and domain-specific inductive biases.
papers.abstract: Generative models typically rely on either simple latent priors (e.g., Variational Autoencoders, VAEs), which are efficient but limited, or highly expressive iterative samplers (e.g., Diffusion and Energy-based Models), which are costly and opaque. We introduce the Kolmogorov-Arnold Energy Model (KAEM) to bridge this trade-off and provide a new avenue for latent-space interpretability. Based on a novel interpretation of the Kolmogorov-Arnold Representation Theorem, which provides new structural biases for generative modeling, KAEM imposes a univariate latent structure that enables fast and exact inference via the inverse transform method. With a low-dimensional latent space and appropriate inductive biases, we show that importance sampling becomes a viable, unbiased, and highly efficient posterior inference method. For settings where importance sampling fails, we propose a population-based strategy that decomposes the posterior into a sequence of annealed distributions to improve mixing during sampling, a common pitfall in Energy-based Models. We present initial comparisons of KAEM against VAEs for the SVHN and CelebA datasets, demonstrating its potential for competitive sample quality, inference speed, and interpretability.

papers.title: Rewire-then-Probe: A Contrastive Recipe for Probing Biomedical Knowledge of Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how to effectively probe biomedical knowledge from pre-trained language models, addressing domain-specific challenges such as multi-token entities and vocabulary bias.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces MedLAMA, a biomedical knowledge probing benchmark, and Contrastive-Probe, a self-supervised method that improves probing performance by rewiring PLMs without using probing data.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents MedLAMA and Contrastive-Probe, showing that PLMs can be rewired to better probe biomedical knowledge, though evaluation criteria may underestimate their capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Existing probing methods achieve less than 3% acc@10 on MedLAMA due to challenges like multi-token answers.
Contrastive-Probe improves acc@10 to 24% by rewiring PLMs with self-supervised contrastive learning.
Different PLMs perform better on different types of relational knowledge, reflecting their training corpora.
Transformer layers encode different types of information, with optimal probing performance varying by relation and layer.
Human evaluation reveals that UMLS does not cover all factual knowledge, suggesting PLMs encode richer information than benchmarked.
papers.limitation:
Difficulty in early stopping due to different optimal training steps for different models and datasets.
Performance variance with different contrastive tuning corpora and random seeds.
future_direction: Integrating encoding space and input space optimization for better probing.
Improving the stability of Contrastive-Probe and investigating its nature.
Exploring layer-wise and relation-wise training for knowledge infusion.
papers.abstract: Knowledge probing is crucial for understanding the knowledge transfer mechanism behind the pre-trained language models (PLMs). Despite the growing progress of probing knowledge for PLMs in the general domain, specialised areas such as biomedical domain are vastly under-explored. To catalyse the research in this direction, we release a well-curated biomedical knowledge probing benchmark, MedLAMA, which is constructed based on the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) Metathesaurus. We test a wide spectrum of state-of-the-art PLMs and probing approaches on our benchmark, reaching at most 3% of acc@10. While highlighting various sources of domain-specific challenges that amount to this underwhelming performance, we illustrate that the underlying PLMs have a higher potential for probing tasks. To achieve this, we propose Contrastive-Probe, a novel self-supervised contrastive probing approach, that adjusts the underlying PLMs without using any probing data. While Contrastive-Probe pushes the acc@10 to 28%, the performance gap still remains notable. Our human expert evaluation suggests that the probing performance of our Contrastive-Probe is still under-estimated as UMLS still does not include the full spectrum of factual knowledge. We hope MedLAMA and Contrastive-Probe facilitate further developments of more suited probing techniques for this domain.

papers.title: Modelling Cellular Perturbations with the Sparse Additive Mechanism Shift Variational Autoencoder
papers.research_question: How to model the effects of diverse interventions on cells to characterize unknown biological mechanisms of action, combining compositionality, disentanglement, and interpretability for perturbation models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SAMS-VAE, a generative model that combines sparsity, compositionality, and disentanglement for perturbation modeling, demonstrating improved predictive performance and interpretability on single-cell sequencing data.
papers.conclusion: SAMS-VAE is a useful model for perturbational screening data, with improved predictive performance and ability to recover factors correlated with biological mechanisms, and may aid in scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
SAMS-VAE with correlated inference achieves the best test IWELBO and average treatment effect correlation.
SAMS-VAE's latent mask is more predictive of annotated biological pathways than SVAE+.
SAMS-VAE and CPA-VAE perform well on out-of-distribution combinatorial tasks and in low-data settings.
SAMS-VAE improves prediction of nonlinear genetic interactions over a naive linear model.
Correlated inference strategies (correlated zbasal and correlated E) improve model performance.
papers.limitation: The prior on the mask may not enforce sparsity as desired when sample size increases, requiring adjustment of the prior strength to achieve desired sparsity.
future_direction: Studying how perturbations interact and compose in more complex fashion.
Incorporating different forms of prior knowledge into such systems.
papers.abstract: Generative models of observations under interventions have been a vibrant topic of interest across machine learning and the sciences in recent years. For example, in drug discovery, there is a need to model the effects of diverse interventions on cells in order to characterize unknown biological mechanisms of action. We propose the Sparse Additive Mechanism Shift Variational Autoencoder, SAMS-VAE, to combine compositionality, disentanglement, and interpretability for perturbation models. SAMS-VAE models the latent state of a perturbed sample as the sum of a local latent variable capturing sample-specific variation and sparse global variables of latent intervention effects. Crucially, SAMS-VAE sparsifies these global latent variables for individual perturbations to identify disentangled, perturbation-specific latent subspaces that are flexibly composable. We evaluate SAMS-VAE both quantitatively and qualitatively on a range of tasks using two popular single cell sequencing datasets. In order to measure perturbation-specific model-properties, we also introduce a framework for evaluation of perturbation models based on average treatment effects with links to posterior predictive checks. SAMS-VAE outperforms comparable models in terms of generalization across in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks, including a combinatorial reasoning task under resource paucity, and yields interpretable latent structures which correlate strongly to known biological mechanisms. Our results suggest SAMS-VAE is an interesting addition to the modeling toolkit for machine learning-driven scientific discovery.

papers.title: A Functional Information Perspective on Model Interpretation
papers.research_question: How can we measure the contribution of input features to a model's decision function using a functional information perspective that accounts for feature correlations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a theoretical framework for model interpretability based on functional entropy and functional Fisher information, which provides a principled way to measure feature contributions while accounting for data covariance.
papers.conclusion: The functional information perspective provides a theoretical foundation for sampling-based interpretability methods and demonstrates efficacy across multiple data modalities.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method outperforms existing sampling-based interpretability methods (SmoothGrad, SmoothGradSQ, VarGrad) on audio, image, and text modalities in post-hoc consistency evaluations.
The method provides more interpretable explanations by highlighting unique characteristic features for each class (e.g., lion's mouth, zebra's stripes).
The covariance matrix plays a significant role, especially for continuous data like audio and images, improving explanation quality.
The method reveals different patterns of token contributions across different text architectures (LSTM, BiLSTM, CNN, transformer).
The method fails to effectively explain transformer architectures, likely due to tight connections from the attention mechanism.
papers.limitation:
The covariance matrix may impose heavy memory requirements.
The method fails to explain transformer architectures effectively.
future_direction: Explore the importance of the feature covariance matrix more deeply across different cases.
Develop effective and efficient approximations to mitigate the memory requirements of the covariance matrix.
papers.abstract: Contemporary predictive models are hard to interpret as their deep nets exploit numerous complex relations between input elements. This work suggests a theoretical framework for model interpretability by measuring the contribution of relevant features to the functional entropy of the network with respect to the input. We rely on the log-Sobolev inequality that bounds the functional entropy by the functional Fisher information with respect to the covariance of the data. This provides a principled way to measure the amount of information contribution of a subset of features to the decision function. Through extensive experiments, we show that our method surpasses existing interpretability sampling-based methods on various data signals such as image, text, and audio.

papers.title: A Spectral Theory of Neural Prediction and Alignment
papers.research_question: Why do many different deep neural networks yield similar neural predictions, and how can we differentiate among models that perform equally well at predicting neural responses?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a spectral theory that decomposes neural prediction error into model eigenspectra and alignment with neural data, and provides geometric measures (error mode radius Rem and dimension Dem) to interpret the error, revealing that different models can achieve similar prediction error through different geometric properties.
papers.conclusion: The spectral theory provides a framework to interpret neural prediction error and shows that geometric measures can differentiate models with similar prediction error, guiding future experiments and model design for improved neural activity prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The spectral theory accurately predicts neural prediction error for ridge regression from model activations to neural responses.
Error mode geometry (Rem and Dem) varies across models even when they have similar neural prediction error, providing additional insight into how models achieve low error.
Early model stages predict early visual areas (V1/V2) better, while later stages predict downstream areas (V4/IT) better, aligning with the hierarchical organization of the visual cortex.
Trained models have better alignment (Wi) with neural data than randomly initialized models, which is the main driver of improved prediction error.
Adversarial training improves alignment between model eigenvectors and early visual cortex activity, leading to lower prediction error in early areas.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical predictions are only accurate in the large P limit (large number of stimuli), and the tail eigenvalues of the empirical Gram matrix are often underestimated.
The results depend on the stimulus set used, which affects the model eigenspectra and thus the error mode geometry.
future_direction: Future work could consider choosing stimulus sets to maximize the difference between model eigenspectra, leading to greater differences in neural predictions.
Extending the theory to other regression methods and non-linear mappings between model activations and neural responses.
Applying the geometric measures to other domains beyond visual cortex to understand model representations more broadly.
papers.abstract: The representations of neural networks are often compared to those of biological systems by performing regression between the neural network responses and those measured from biological systems. Many different state-of-the-art deep neural networks yield similar neural predictions, but it remains unclear how to differentiate among models that perform equally well at predicting neural responses. To gain insight into this, we use a recent theoretical framework that relates the generalization error from regression to the spectral properties of the model and the target. We apply this theory to the case of regression between model activations and neural responses and decompose the neural prediction error in terms of the model eigenspectra, alignment of model eigenvectors and neural responses, and the training set size. Using this decomposition, we introduce geometrical measures to interpret the neural prediction error. We test a large number of deep neural networks that predict visual cortical activity and show that there are multiple types of geometries that result in low neural prediction error as measured via regression. The work demonstrates that carefully decomposing representational metrics can provide interpretability of how models are capturing neural activity and points the way towards improved models of neural activity.

papers.title: Latent Space Characterization of Autoencoder Variants
papers.research_question: How do the latent spaces of different autoencoder variants (CAE, DAE, VAE) structure themselves, and how do they change with input perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper characterizes the latent spaces of autoencoders as product manifolds, showing that CAEs and DAEs have stratified non-smooth manifolds due to rank variability, while VAEs have smooth manifolds with consistent ranks, and provides an alternate view via Hilbert space transformation.
papers.conclusion: The latent spaces of CAEs and DAEs are non-smooth stratified manifolds, whereas VAEs have smooth product manifolds, as evidenced by manifold, Hilbert space, and t-SNE analyses.
papers.key_findings:
CAE and DAE latent spaces form stratified manifolds with varying ranks of SPSD matrices, leading to non-smooth structure.
VAE latent space is a smooth product manifold with fixed ranks across noise levels.
In Hilbert space, CAE and DAE subspaces change dimensionality and orientation with noise, while VAE subspaces remain constant.
t-SNE visualization shows divergence between clean and noisy points for CAE and DAE, but tight clustering for VAE.
PSNR decreases with noise for CAE and DAE, but is maintained for VAE, correlating with subspace dimensionality.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other autoencoder variants and more datasets.
Characterize latent spaces of other generative models.
Devise denoising and deblurring algorithms based on manifold structure.
papers.abstract: Understanding the latent spaces learned by deep learning models is crucial in exploring how they represent and generate complex data. Autoencoders (AEs) have played a key role in the area of representation learning, with numerous regularization techniques and training principles developed not only to enhance their ability to learn compact and robust representations, but also to reveal how different architectures influence the structure and smoothness of the lower-dimensional non-linear manifold. We strive to characterize the structure of the latent spaces learned by different autoencoders including convolutional autoencoders (CAEs), denoising autoencoders (DAEs), and variational autoencoders (VAEs) and how they change with the perturbations in the input. By characterizing the matrix manifolds corresponding to the latent spaces, we provide an explanation for the well-known observation that the latent spaces of CAE and DAE form non-smooth manifolds, while that of VAE forms a smooth manifold. We also map the points of the matrix manifold to a Hilbert space using distance preserving transforms and provide an alternate view in terms of the subspaces generated in the Hilbert space as a function of the distortion in the input. The results show that the latent manifolds of CAE and DAE are stratified with each stratum being a smooth product manifold, while the manifold of VAE is a smooth product manifold of two symmetric positive definite matrices and a symmetric positive semi-definite matrix.

papers.title: A PCA-like Autoencoder
papers.research_question: How can we create an autoencoder with a latent space where components are ordered by importance and are statistically independent, similar to PCA but with non-linear transformations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a novel autoencoder architecture and training algorithm that learns a latent space with components ordered by importance and statistically independent, enabling meaningful interpolation.
papers.conclusion: The PCA Autoencoder learns an interpretable latent space where components are independent and ordered by importance, allowing for meaningful interpolation with respect to data properties.
papers.key_findings:
The PCA Autoencoder learns a latent space where the first component corresponds to the surface area of ellipses, and the second corresponds to the ratio between the two axes.
For ellipses with three parameters (axes and rotation), the PCA Autoencoder learns a first axis for surface area and subsequent axes for axis ratios in different directions, separating geometric attributes.
The standard autoencoder mixes geometric attributes in its latent space, making it less interpretable.
The PCA Autoencoder fails to fully separate attributes for disks with varying radius and grayscale, where the second axis mixes both size and grey-scale.
papers.limitation: The algorithm increases the latent space size by one dimension at each step, which can be problematic for learning representations that require multiple dimensions simultaneously (e.g., object position).
future_direction: Extend the method to more complex data.
Consider increasing the latent space by packets of codes to allow more freedom in learning representations, while finding an efficient way to compute the covariance loss for these packets.
papers.abstract: An autoencoder is a neural network which data projects to and from a lower dimensional latent space, where this data is easier to understand and model. The autoencoder consists of two sub-networks, the encoder and the decoder, which carry out these transformations. The neural network is trained such that the output is as close to the input as possible, the data having gone through an information bottleneck : the latent space. This tool bears significant ressemblance to Principal Component Analysis (PCA), with two main differences. Firstly, the autoencoder is a non-linear transformation, contrary to PCA, which makes the autoencoder more flexible and powerful. Secondly, the axes found by a PCA are orthogonal, and are ordered in terms of the amount of variability which the data presents along these axes. This makes the interpretability of the PCA much greater than that of the autoencoder, which does not have these attributes. Ideally, then, we would like an autoencoder whose latent space consists of independent components, ordered by decreasing importance to the data. In this paper, we propose an algorithm to create such a network. We create an iterative algorithm which progressively increases the size of the latent space, learning a new dimension at each step. Secondly, we propose a covariance loss term to add to the standard autoencoder loss function, as well as a normalisation layer just before the latent space, which encourages the latent space components to be statistically independent. We demonstrate the results of this autoencoder on simple geometric shapes, and find that the algorithm indeed finds a meaningful representation in the latent space. This means that subsequent interpolation in the latent space has meaning with respect to the geometric properties of the images.

papers.title: Multi-scale Graph Autoregressive Modeling: Molecular Property Prediction via Next Token Prediction
papers.research_question: How can we bridge the gap between graph topology preservation and scalable autoregressive training to enable decoder-only Transformers to learn molecular graphs via next-token prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Connection-Aware Motif Sequencing (CamS), a graph-to-sequence representation that enables decoder-only Transformers to learn molecular graphs via next-token prediction, achieving state-of-the-art performance on molecular property prediction benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CamS bridges the gap between graph topology and autoregressive training, enabling effective molecular property prediction via next-token prediction with a standard decoder-only Transformer backbone.
papers.key_findings:
CamS-LLaMA achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoleculeNet and MoleculeACE benchmarks.
Multi-scale concatenation is the key driver of performance.
The causal serialization effectively drives attention toward cliff-determining structural differences.
CamS provides a more nuanced structural discrimination than descriptor-based approaches like KPGT.
The method combines general-purpose robustness with fine-grained structural discriminability.
papers.limitation: Vocabulary materialization involves expensive subgraph-isomorphism matching that prohibits direct training on billion-scale corpora.
papers.abstract: We present Connection-Aware Motif Sequencing (CamS), a graph-to-sequence representation that enables decoder-only Transformers to learn molecular graphs via standard next-token prediction (NTP). For molecular property prediction, SMILES-based NTP scales well but lacks explicit topology, whereas graph-native masked modeling captures connectivity but risks disrupting the pivotal chemical details (e.g., activity cliffs). CamS bridges this gap by serializing molecular graphs into structure-rich causal sequences. CamS first mines data-driven connection-aware motifs. It then serializes motifs via scaffold-rooted breadth-first search (BFS) to establish a stable core-to-periphery order. Crucially, CamS enables hierarchical modeling by concatenating sequences from fine to coarse motif scales, allowing the model to condition global scaffolds on dense, uncorrupted local structural evidence. We instantiate CamS-LLaMA by pre-training a vanilla LLaMA backbone on CamS sequences. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoleculeNet and the activity-cliff benchmark MoleculeACE, outperforming both SMILES-based language models and strong graph baselines. Interpretability analysis confirms that our multi-scale causal serialization effectively drives attention toward cliff-determining differences.

papers.title: Capturing the Development of Internal Representations in a High-Performing Deep Network for Sleep Stage Classification
papers.research_question: How does the ability to differentiate sleep stages develop across the layers of a deep convolutional neural network, and how can this be quantified using visualization and kernel alignment methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a deep convolutional neural network for sleep stage classification that achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, and introduces a max-pooling CKA approach to quantify the development of sleep stage specialization and differentiation across network layers.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a high-accuracy CNN for sleep stage classification and demonstrates through t-SNE and max-pooling CKA that sleep stage specialization and differentiation abilities increase monotonically with network layer depth.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN achieves 84.50% accuracy on sleep stage classification, exceeding human inter-scorer agreement of 82.6%.
Including wake data before and after sleep improves performance on wake epochs, but mid-sleep wake epochs are harder to classify.
Visualization with t-SNE shows increasing class separation with layer depth.
Max-pooling CKA provides quantitative measures that validate t-SNE and show monotonic improvement in stage specialization and differentiation with depth.
The network's internal representations gradually develop sleep stage differentiation, with partial differentiation even in shallow layers.
papers.limitation:
Performance is weakest on the under-represented sleep stage S1, and oversampling did not significantly improve it.
Models with more input channels may require more data to achieve optimal generalization compared to single-channel models.
future_direction: Investigating the use of CKA with nonlinear kernels.
Applying the proposed techniques to alternative network types such as recurrent neural networks.
Simultaneous and complementary use of CKA-based quantification and activation maximization approaches.
papers.abstract: Abstract Deep neural networks can provide accurate automated classification of human sleep signals into sleep stages that enables more effective diagnosis and treatment of sleep disorders.
