In the ADRB2 dataset, the model achieves perfect accuracy but very low attribution-AUC, indicating it does not learn the correct binding logic.
The framework provides a test for dataset bias given a hypothesis, indicating when models must be simplified/regularized or datasets augmented.
papers.limitation: Attributions offer a reductive view of the model's internal logic and fail to capture higher-order feature interactions.
future_direction: Further research to reveal feature interactions in the model's predictions.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracy at classifying molecules with respect to whether they bind to specific protein targets. A key breakthrough would occur if these models could reveal the fragment pharmacophores that are causally involved in binding. Extracting chemical details of binding from the networks could enable scientific discoveries about the mechanisms of drug actions. However, doing so requires shining light into the black box that is the trained neural network model, a task that has proved difficult across many domains. Here we show how the binding mechanism learned by deep neural network models can be interrogated, using a recently described attribution method. We first work with carefully constructed synthetic datasets, in which the molecular features responsible for "binding" are fully known. We find that networks that achieve perfect accuracy on held-out test datasets still learn spurious correlations, and we are able to exploit this nonrobustness to construct adversarial examples that fool the model. This makes these models unreliable for accurately revealing information about the mechanisms of protein-ligand binding. In light of our findings, we prescribe a test that checks whether a hypothesized mechanism can be learned. If the test fails, it indicates that the model must be simplified or regularized and/or that the training dataset requires augmentation.

papers.title: From Neurons to Neutrons: A Case Study in Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability extract scientific knowledge from neural networks trained on physics data, and can such insights align with human-derived domain knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can extract scientifically meaningful representations from neural networks trained on nuclear physics data, aligning with human-derived concepts like the semi-empirical mass formula and shell model.
papers.conclusion: These findings provide a proof-of-concept that neural networks, when trained on scientific data, can learn useful representations that align with human knowledge, opening exciting possibilities for future research on richer data and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings of proton and neutron numbers exhibit a helix structure that encodes nuclear physics concepts like the volume and asymmetry terms.
The orderedness of embeddings along the first principal component correlates with generalization performance.
Penultimate layer features correspond to terms in the semi-empirical mass formula and nuclear shell model.
Latent space topography reveals the algorithm used by the model for binding energy prediction, geometrically representing the SEMF.
Models trained on nuclear data learn representations similar to those trained on pseudo data from human-derived theory.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted knowledge is not guaranteed; representations may be complex and not easily distilled into interpretable theories.
Lack of quantitative metrics to assess interpretability.
Symbolic regression from neural features did not yield fully interpretable improvements over human-derived models.
Requires interdisciplinary collaborations and close partnerships between machine learning researchers and domain experts.
future_direction: Applying interpretability to richer data and more complex tasks.
Developing quantitative metrics for interpretability.
Exploring other scientific domains for knowledge extraction.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) promises a path toward fully understanding how neural networks make their predictions. Prior work demonstrates that even when trained to perform simple arithmetic, models can implement a variety of algorithms (sometimes concurrently) depending on initialization and hyperparameters. Does this mean neuron-level interpretability techniques have limited applicability? We argue that high-dimensional neural networks can learn low-dimensional representations of their training data that are useful beyond simply making good predictions. Such representations can be understood through the mechanistic interpretability lens and provide insights that are surprisingly faithful to human-derived domain knowledge. This indicates that such approaches to interpretability can be useful for deriving a new understanding of a problem from models trained to solve it. As a case study, we extract nuclear physics concepts by studying models trained to reproduce nuclear data.

papers.title: Occupancies vs Embeddings: Internal representations of Ab Initio and Graph Probabilistic Models*
papers.research_question: To what degree does the end-to-end data-driven approach (graph neural networks) coalesce with traditional ab initio predictions of molecular behavior? Does the model contain internal characteristics of the wave function or electron density from DFT?
papers.core_contribution: This study compares atomwise representations from graph neural networks (GNNs) and ab initio density functional theory (DFT), revealing that GNN embeddings offer higher resolution and can accurately predict DFT-derived atomic occupancy values, whereas the reverse mapping is significantly less accurate.
papers.conclusion: GNN embeddings serve as a richer, more informative molecular representation than DFT-derived atomic occupancies, demonstrating the power of end-to-end statistical models to encapsulate and extend traditional quantum chemical information, though further exploration is needed regarding their robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.key_findings:
Both GNN embedding vectors and DFT-derived atomic occupancy vectors can separate and label chemical environments, but embeddings provide much higher resolution and lower classification error.
Embedding vectors can predict atomic occupancy values with high accuracy (MAE 2.5e-3, R2 0.996), but the reverse mapping from occupancies to embeddings is an order of magnitude less accurate (MAE 0.235, R2 0.379).
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reveals qualitative similarities in the eigenvalue spectra between the two representations, but the embedding space captures more nuanced information.
The embedding representation contains more information than the occupancy representation, enabling precise mapping to occupancies but not vice versa within the same model chemistry.
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) shows embeddings achieve near-perfect functional group classification, while occupancy vectors show higher error, especially for similar chemical environments.
papers.limitation: Interatomic information was omitted due to the need to respect rotational equivariance for the embeddings, and the use of Mulliken population analysis might hamper a faithful analysis of the information content in the occupancies.
future_direction: Further studies to tighten conclusions about the relationship between embeddings and electron density.
Exploration of GNN embeddings' robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Chemical modeling has traditionally been separated into two fairly non-overlapping frameworks: the exact framework of \textit{ab initio} models and the data-driven framework of statistical models. However, recent advances in machine learning approaches have intercepted the exact \textit{ab initio} frameworks by using an \textit{end-to-end} probabilistic model of the Schr\"odinger equation in the Born-Oppenheimer approximation---from raw nuclear configurations to quantum observables such as the energy. While probabilistic modelling offers promising advancements to speed up computational predictions, the internal representation and its connection to the underlying quantum data---the wave function or electron density---which they implicitly rely on for training, remains relatively poorly understood. This study seeks to make a first comparison of the internal representation from a probabilistic end-to-end models with those from pure \textit{ab initio} frameworks such as density functional theory. We do this by comparing the internal atomwise representation of graph models, also called embeddings, to their most natural \textit{ab initio} counterpart, electron occupancy values. Our findings show that the embedding representations can be employed to transfer learn atomic occupancy values whereas the reverse mapping appears to be less accurate. We discuss the assumption that the probabilistic model could infer the existence of an underlying electron density underpinning the computational \textit{ab-initio} data.

papers.title: DeepFRI Demystified: Interpretability vs. Accuracy in AI Protein Function Prediction
papers.research_question: How interpretable and robust is the DeepFRI model for protein function prediction, and how do different explainability methods compare in highlighting influential residues?
papers.core_contribution: The study reveals that DeepFRI's predictions prioritize conserved structural motifs over functional residues, and different explainability methods offer varying levels of granularity, highlighting trade-offs between accuracy and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: DeepFRI has strengths in conserved domains but limitations in complex proteins, and interpretability methods must be chosen carefully to balance robustness and precision for biological insights.
papers.key_findings:
DeepFRI's predictions often prioritize structural motifs like beta sheets over functional residues, leading to potential misinterpretations.
GradCAM provides broad heatmaps with low sparsity, Excitation Backpropagation offers binary masks with high sparsity, and PGExplainer gives precise per-residue scores.
The model is robust to mutations, requiring over 200 mutations in some cases to cause misclassification, but this may overlook biologically significant changes.
Sparsity analysis shows that explainability methods vary significantly, with GradCAM being the least sparse and Excitation Backpropagation the most sparse.
Using an ensemble of explainability methods can highlight high-confidence residues and areas of epistemic uncertainty.
papers.limitation:
DeepFRI prioritizes structural motifs over functional residues, potentially leading to inaccurate interpretations of protein function.
The model's robustness to mutations may cause it to overlook biologically significant changes unless a large fraction of the structure is disrupted.
DeepFRI's message-passing can overlook long-range or allosteric effects in complex regulatory proteins.
future_direction: Guide experimental validation through targeted mutagenesis based on explainability results.
Fuse GCN topology with per-residue embeddings from protein language models for improved sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Machine learning technologies for protein function prediction are black box models. Despite their potential to identify key drug targets with high accuracy and accelerate therapy development, the adoption of these methods depends on verifying their findings. This study evaluates DeepFRI, a leading Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) based tool, using advanced explainability techniques (GradCAM, Excitation Backpropagation, and PGExplainer) and adversarial robustness tests. Our findings reveal that the model's predictions often prioritize conserved motifs over truly deterministic residues, complicating the identification of functional sites. Quantitative analyses show that explainability methods differ significantly in granularity, with GradCAM providing broad relevance and PGExplainer pinpointing specific active sites. These results highlight tradeoffs between accuracy and interpretability, suggesting areas for improvement in DeepFRI's architecture to enhance its trustworthiness in drug discovery and regulatory settings.

papers.title: Brain-optimized deep neural network models of human visual areas learn non-hierarchical representations
papers.research_question: Does hierarchical representation in deep neural networks (DNNs) improve the accuracy of predicting brain activity in human visual areas V1-V4?
papers.core_contribution: Hierarchical representations are not necessary to accurately predict human brain activity in V1-V4, and DNNs with diverse architectures (from strict serial hierarchies to multiple independent branches) can encode brain-like visual representations.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that hierarchical representations are not necessary for accurately predicting brain activity in human visual areas V1-V4, and brain-optimized DNNs can learn non-hierarchical representations while maintaining high accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Brain-optimized DNNs (GNet) predict brain activity in V1-V4 more accurately than task-optimized AlexNet for both natural and artificial stimuli.
Single-branch (GNet8j) and multi-branch (GNet8r) brain-optimized models yield similar prediction accuracy despite architectural differences.
Both single-branch and multi-branch models exhibit integration hierarchy, with receptive field sizes expanding from V1 to V4.
Only single-branch models (AlexNet and GNet8j) learn compositional and entailment hierarchies; multi-branch models (GNet8r) do not.
Hierarchical representations are not essential for accurate prediction of brain activity, as non-hierarchical models can achieve state-of-the-art accuracy.
papers.limitation: The best models leave much variance unexplained, accounting for at most 78% of explainable variance in brain activity.
future_direction: Developing new analytical tools for uncovering the function of representations encoded in different human visual areas using brain-optimized networks.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) optimized for visual tasks learn representations that align layer depth with the hierarchy of visual areas in the primate brain. One interpretation of this finding is that hierarchical representations are necessary to accurately predict brain activity in the primate visual system. To test this interpretation, we optimized DNNs to directly predict brain activity measured with fMRI in human visual areas V1-V4. We trained a single-branch DNN to predict activity in all four visual areas jointly, and a multi-branch DNN to predict each visual area independently. Although it was possible for the multi-branch DNN to learn hierarchical representations, only the single-branch DNN did so. This result shows that hierarchical representations are not necessary to accurately predict human brain activity in V1-V4, and that DNNs that encode brain-like visual representations may differ widely in their architecture, ranging from strict serial hierarchies to multiple independent branches.

papers.title: Scale-invariant feature extraction of neural network and renormalization group flow
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) and renormalization group (RG) flow, and how does the RBM learn to extract features from spin configurations?
papers.core_contribution: The unsupervised RBM trained on Ising model configurations at various temperatures generates a flow of temperature that approaches the critical point Tc, opposite to the typical RG flow, indicating the RBM learns scale-invariant features.
papers.conclusion: The RBM flow is attracted to the critical point when trained on a wide range of temperatures, and the RBM learns scale-invariant features, showing a connection to RG but with an opposite flow direction.
papers.key_findings:
For type V RBM (trained on configurations from T=0 to T=6), the temperature flow approaches the critical temperature Tc=2.27, making Tc a stable fixed point.
When the hidden layer size Nh is less than or equal to the visible layer size Nv, the flow stabilizes at Tc; for Nh > Nv, the flow eventually moves towards high temperature.
The weight matrix product WW^T reflects spin correlations, and its off-diagonal components decay similarly to spin correlations near Tc.
The eigenvalue spectrum of WW^T for type V RBM shows a gradual decrease without jumps, suggesting scale-invariant feature learning.
The RBM flow is attracted to the features it has learned during training, e.g., type H/L RBMs flow towards high/low temperatures respectively.
future_direction: Investigate the RBM flow for first-order phase transitions, e.g., in the Blume-Capel model.
Study the attractor of RBM flows for human faces to understand value judgments.
Describe the RBM flow as a stochastic process using Langevin or Fokker-Planck equations.
papers.abstract: Theoretical understanding of how a deep neural network (DNN) extracts features from input images is still unclear, but it is widely believed that the extraction is performed hierarchically through a process of coarse graining. It reminds us of the basic renormalization group (RG) concept in statistical physics. In order to explore possible relations between DNN and RG, we use the restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) applied to an Ising model and construct a flow of model parameters (in particular, temperature) generated by the RBM. We show that the unsupervised RBM trained by spin configurations at various temperatures from T=0 to T=6 generates a flow along which the temperature approaches the critical value T_{c}=2.27. This behavior is the opposite of the typical RG flow of the Ising model. By analyzing various properties of the weight matrices of the trained RBM, we discuss why it flows towards T_{c} and how the RBM learns to extract features of spin configurations.

papers.title: This Looks Like That... Does it? Shortcomings of Latent Space Prototype Interpretability in Deep Networks
papers.research_question: Does the similarity in latent space used by prototype-based models correspond to human-interpretable similarity in input space? The paper investigates the semantic gap that can corrupt interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that prototype-based interpretability methods suffer from a semantic gap between latent space similarity and human-interpretable input space similarity, which can be corrupted by adversarial noise or compression artefacts.
papers.conclusion: Practitioners should be cautious when using prototype-based models, especially in sensitive domains like medical imaging, because the interpretability can break down in the presence of adversarial noise or compression artefacts.
papers.key_findings:
Small adversarial perturbations can cause ProtoPNet to identify prototypes in arbitrary, non-sensical locations while maintaining correct classification.
JPEG compression artefacts can cause ProtoPNet to assign drastically different similarity scores to visually similar image patches, breaking the interpretability.
The interpretability mechanism is not robust to common data corruptions.
Adversarial training and data augmentation can partially mitigate these issues but at the cost of accuracy.
future_direction: More comprehensive study of the robustness of interpretability mechanisms.
Examination of interpretable architectures different to ProtoPNets.
Identification of further sources of artefacts/noise that may lead to a break down of interpretability in real-world settings.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks that yield human interpretable decisions by architectural design have lately become an increasingly popular alternative to post hoc interpretation of traditional black-box models. Among these networks, the arguably most widespread approach is so-called prototype learning, where similarities to learned latent prototypes serve as the basis of classifying an unseen data point. In this work, we point to an important shortcoming of such approaches. Namely, there is a semantic gap between similarity in latent space and similarity in input space, which can corrupt interpretability. We design two experiments that exemplify this issue on the so-called ProtoPNet. Specifically, we find that this network's interpretability mechanism can be led astray by intentionally crafted or even JPEG compression artefacts, which can produce incomprehensible decisions. We argue that practitioners ought to have this shortcoming in mind when deploying prototype-based models in practice.

papers.title: It's FLAN time! Summing feature-wise latent representations for interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we build interpretable deep learning models that retain the representational power of neural networks while being interpretable by design?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FLANs, a class of structurally constrained neural networks that are interpretable by design, achieving reasonable performance on complex datasets without needing post-hoc interpretation methods.
papers.conclusion: FLANs are a powerful and interpretable model class that can be natively interpreted without post-hoc methods, representing an important step towards interpretable machine learning in complex domains.
papers.key_findings:
FLANs achieve comparable performance to established models on a series of benchmark datasets across tabular, image, and text domains.
FLANs provide native interpretability through feature importance (via latent norms) and example-based explanations without the need for post-hoc methods.
FLANs may have difficulties in learning complex/long interactions, as seen in the CUB and IMDb datasets, but can still achieve 100% training accuracy, indicating the ability to learn complex interactions that may not generalize.
papers.limitation: FLANs may have difficulties in learning complex/long interactions, as seen in the CUB and IMDb datasets.
future_direction: Address the generalization difficulties of the model.
Run user studies to further validate the interpretability of the model.
papers.abstract: Interpretability has become a necessary feature for machine learning models deployed in critical scenarios, e.g. legal system, healthcare. In these situations, algorithmic decisions may have (potentially negative) long-lasting effects on the end-user affected by the decision. In many cases, the representational power of deep learning models is not needed, therefore simple and interpretable models (e.g. linear models) should be preferred. However, in high-dimensional and/or complex domains (e.g. computer vision), the universal approximation capabilities of neural networks are required. Inspired by linear models and the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, we propose a novel class of structurally-constrained neural networks, which we call FLANs (Feature-wise Latent Additive Networks). Crucially, FLANs process each input feature separately, computing for each of them a representation in a common latent space. These feature-wise latent representations are then simply summed, and the aggregated representation is used for prediction. These constraints (which are at the core of the interpretability of linear models) allow a user to estimate the effect of each individual feature independently from the others, enhancing interpretability. In a set of experiments across different domains, we show how without compromising excessively the test performance, the structural constraints proposed in FLANs indeed facilitates the interpretability of deep learning models. We quantitatively compare FLANs interpretability to post-hoc methods using recently introduced metrics, discussing the advantages of natively interpretable models over a post-hoc analysis.

papers.title: Deep learning features encode interpretable morphologies within histological images
papers.research_question: What is the interpretability of CNN-derived image features (mones) in histopathological images, and can they be linearly correlated with biological phenotypes and gene expression?
papers.core_contribution: CNN-derived features (mones) are interpretable and linearly correlated with biological phenotypes and gene expression, enabling interpretable analysis without a trained classifier.
papers.conclusion: Mones offer a powerful approach for interpreting deep learning models in histopathology, linking image features to biological processes.
papers.key_findings:
Individual mones can differentiate phenotypes (e.g., tumor vs normal) with statistical significance.
Mones form clusters with strong correlations that are preserved across related cancer types.
Linear models based on mones can accurately classify tumors and cancer types (high AUC).
Mones have interpretable correlations with gene expression, e.g., collagen genes in ovarian cancer and immune genes in colon and lung cancers.
Mone analysis provides interpretability without requiring a trained classifier.
papers.limitation:
Correlation does not imply causation.
Some mones' ability to distinguish tumor from normal is impacted by differences between frozen and FFPE modalities.
future_direction: Investigate the utility of mones for other image analysis tasks, such as survival prediction and virtual staining.
Integrate mones with other data modalities, such as genomic and clinical data, to enhance interpretability and predictive power.

papers.title: Evaluating Self-Supervised Learning for Molecular Graph Embeddings
papers.research_question: How can we effectively evaluate graph self-supervised learning (GSSL) methods for molecular graph embeddings, given that their broad applicability complicates evaluation and current downstream datasets may not provide a complete picture?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MOLGRAPH EVAL, a benchmark for evaluating molecular graph embeddings from GSSL methods via a suite of probing tasks, revealing significant inconsistencies between inferences from existing downstream datasets and more nuanced probing.
papers.conclusion: MOLGRAPH EVAL provides a more comprehensive and nuanced evaluation of GSSL methods for molecular graphs, uncovering limitations of current evaluation methodologies that rely solely on downstream task performance.
papers.key_findings:
All GSSL methods improve molecular property prediction (MPP) over random initialization, but the performance gain varies with dataset size.
Rankings of GSSL methods differ between using fixed embeddings (probing) and fine-tuned embeddings, indicating probing alone is not a definitive indicator for fine-tuning performance.
Optimal pre-training hyperparameters for fixed and fine-tuned embeddings often differ, suggesting that probing fixed embeddings may not reflect true downstream performance after fine-tuning.
Randomly initialized embeddings outperform almost every GSSL method on node- and pair-level topological metrics, indicating GSSL methods are not universally better and random features can be useful for local geometry tasks.
Substructure detection performance correlates well with MPP performance, suggesting that GSSL methods' superiority in MPP may be attributed to their capacity for substructure awareness.
papers.limitation:
The benchmark is limited to the nine studied GSSL methods and the molecular datasets used; extending to more methods and datasets is needed for broader conclusions.
Potential ethical concerns include bias and fairness in the datasets, dual use for designing harmful substances, environmental impact of training, and privacy issues.
future_direction: Extend the benchmark to incorporate more GSSL methods and larger datasets (e.g., ZINC15).
Investigate why optimal pre-training configurations for probing and fine-tuning differ.
Explore the reasons behind the strong performance of randomly initialized embeddings on local topological metrics.
papers.abstract: Graph Self-Supervised Learning (GSSL) provides a robust pathway for acquiring embeddings without expert labelling, a capability that carries profound implications for molecular graphs due to the staggering number of potential molecules and the high cost of obtaining labels. However, GSSL methods are designed not for optimisation within a specific domain but rather for transferability across a variety of downstream tasks. This broad applicability complicates their evaluation. Addressing this challenge, we present "Molecular Graph Representation Evaluation" (MOLGRAPHEVAL), generating detailed profiles of molecular graph embeddings with interpretable and diversified attributes. MOLGRAPHEVAL offers a suite of probing tasks grouped into three categories: (i) generic graph, (ii) molecular substructure, and (iii) embedding space properties. By leveraging MOLGRAPHEVAL to benchmark existing GSSL methods against both current downstream datasets and our suite of tasks, we uncover significant inconsistencies between inferences drawn solely from existing datasets and those derived from more nuanced probing. These findings suggest that current evaluation methodologies fail to capture the entirety of the landscape.

papers.title: “Amide − amine + alcohol = carboxylic acid.” chemical reactions as linear algebraic analogies in graph neural networks
papers.research_question: Do graph neural network (GNN) atom-embeddings exhibit linear algebraic analogies similar to word embeddings in NLP, and how do these analogies relate to chemical reactions and properties?
papers.core_contribution: Atom-embeddings in pretrained graph neural networks exhibit linear algebraic analogies that correspond to chemical reactions, revealing a highly structured latent space that mirrors chemical syntax.
papers.conclusion: The latent space of GNNs in chemistry is highly structured and organized according to chemical syntax, with linear analogies providing a global explanatory framework for chemical transformations and properties.
papers.key_findings:
Atom-embeddings in a pretrained GNN (SchNet) show arithmetic properties allowing linear analogies that represent valid chemical reaction formulas, similar to word analogies in NLP.
Reaction vectors (differences between reactant and product embeddings) are approximately constant for a given reaction type and are colinear for similar reactions (e.g., oxidations).
The linear analogies can be explained by a perturbational replicate model based on neighborhood chemical composition, linking the embedding structure to chemical principles.
The structured embedding space facilitates transfer learning and reveals linear relations in chemical properties like NMR chemical shifts and atomization energies.
The organization of the embedding space has two levels: substructure composition and changes to substructure, with similar changes aligning in direction.
papers.limitation:
The QM9 dataset only includes equilibrium geometries, so the reaction datasets only account for initial and product states, not mechanistic transitions.
Geometry optimization using force fields may introduce non-equilibrium geometries from the perspective of the DFT-trained model.
The replicate model is an approximation and ignores the exact layout of the graph.
future_direction: Mapping out the trajectories of reactions in the latent space to study transition states.
Studying how the global explanatory framework reduces to local explanations on a case-by-case basis.
Improving the replicate model by incorporating the exact graph layout and using the same geometry optimization as the GNN model.
papers.abstract: In deep learning methods, especially in the context of chemistry, there is an increasing urgency to uncover the hidden learning mechanisms often dubbed as "black box." In this work, we show that graph models built on computational chemical data behave similar to natural language processing (NLP) models built on text data. Crucially, we show that atom-embeddings, a.k.a atom-parsed graph neural activation patterns, exhibit arithmetic properties that represent valid reaction formulas. This is very similar to how word-embeddings can be combined to make word analogies, thus preserving the semantic meaning behind the words, as in the famous example "King" - "Man" + "Woman" = "Queen." For instance, we show how the reaction from an alcohol to a carbonyl is represented by a constant vector in the embedding space, implicitly representing "-H<sub>2</sub>." This vector is independent from the particular carbonyl reactant and alcohol product and represents a consistent chemical transformation. Other directions in the embedding space are synonymous with distinct chemical changes (ex. the tautomerization direction). In contrast to natural language processing, we can explain the observed chemical analogies using algebraic manipulations on the local chemical composition that surrounds each atom-embedding. Furthermore, the observations find applications in transfer learning, for instance in the formal structure and prediction of atomistic properties, such as <sup>1</sup>H-NMR and <sup>13</sup>C-NMR. This work is in line with the recent push for interpretable explanations to graph neural network modeling of chemistry and uncovers a latent model of chemistry that is highly structured, consistent, and analogous to chemical syntax.

papers.title: k* Distribution: Evaluating the Latent Space of Deep Neural Networks using Local Neighborhood Analysis
papers.research_question: How can local neighborhood analysis be used to evaluate and visualize the distribution of samples in the latent space of neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the k* distribution, a local neighborhood analysis method for visualizing and understanding the distribution of samples in the latent space of neural networks, identifying three patterns: Fractured, Overlapped, and Clustered.
papers.conclusion: The k* distribution method effectively analyzes latent spaces by identifying three patterns, aiding in the understanding and improvement of neural network representations.
papers.key_findings:
Three distinct patterns of sample distribution in latent space are identified: Fractured (positively skewed k* distribution), Overlapped (uniform k* distribution), and Clustered (negatively skewed k* distribution).
The distribution of samples within the network’s learned latent space significantly varies depending on the class.
The k* distribution can be applied to diverse neural network architectures, various layers, and different data modalities (image, text, audio).
Input transformations such as cropping, noise, rotation, and adversarial attacks affect the latent space distribution, often leading to more fractured patterns.
Models trained on stylized or adversarial data show different latent space distributions compared to standard trained models.
papers.limitation: Sacrifices information about absolute distances between samples due to reliance on nearest-neighbor method
papers.abstract: Most examinations of neural networks' learned latent spaces typically employ dimensionality reduction techniques such as t-SNE or UMAP. These methods distort the local neighborhood in the visualization, making it hard to distinguish the structure of a subset of samples in the latent space. In response to this challenge, we introduce the {k*~distribution} and its corresponding visualization technique This method uses local neighborhood analysis to guarantee the preservation of the structure of sample distributions for individual classes within the subset of the learned latent space. This facilitates easy comparison of different k*~distributions, enabling analysis of how various classes are processed by the same neural network. Our study reveals three distinct distributions of samples within the learned latent space subset: a) Fractured, b) Overlapped, and c) Clustered, providing a more profound understanding of existing contemporary visualizations. Experiments show that the distribution of samples within the network's learned latent space significantly varies depending on the class. Furthermore, we illustrate that our analysis can be applied to explore the latent space of diverse neural network architectures, various layers within neural networks, transformations applied to input samples, and the distribution of training and testing data for neural networks. Thus, the k* distribution should aid in visualizing the structure inside neural networks and further foster their understanding. Project Website is available online at https://shashankkotyan.github.io/k-Distribution/.

papers.title: Representation Learning: A Review and New Perspectives
papers.research_question: What makes one representation better than another? Given an example, how should we compute its representation, i.e. perform feature extraction? Also, what are appropriate objectives for learning good representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reviews recent advances in representation learning and deep learning, and discusses open questions about the objectives for learning good representations, computing representations, and the connections between representation learning, density estimation, and manifold learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that representation learning is a key component for advancing AI, and identifies open questions about the objectives for learning good representations, inference, and the connections to manifold learning and density estimation.
papers.key_findings:
Representation learning is crucial for AI because it can disentangle the underlying explanatory factors in data.
Deep architectures promote feature re-use and abstraction, leading to more expressive and invariant representations.
Unsupervised pre-training and deep learning have led to breakthroughs in speech recognition, object recognition, and natural language processing.
There are many open questions about the appropriate objectives for learning good representations and for performing inference (computing representations).
The geometrical perspective of manifold learning connects representation learning to density estimation and provides insights into the structure of data.
future_direction: Determine appropriate objectives for learning good representations.
Develop methods for computing representations (inference).
Explore the geometrical connections between representation learning, density estimation, and manifold learning.
papers.abstract: The success of machine learning algorithms generally depends on data representation, and we hypothesize that this is because different representations can entangle and hide more or less the different explanatory factors of variation behind the data. Although specific domain knowledge can be used to help design representations, learning with generic priors can also be used, and the quest for AI is motivating the design of more powerful representation-learning algorithms implementing such priors. This paper reviews recent work in the area of unsupervised feature learning and deep learning, covering advances in probabilistic models, auto-encoders, manifold learning, and deep networks. This motivates longer-term unanswered questions about the appropriate objectives for learning good representations, for computing representations (i.e., inference), and the geometrical connections between representation learning, density estimation and manifold learning.

papers.title: Peering inside the black box: Learning the relevance of many-body functions in Neural Network potentials
papers.research_question: How can machine learned coarse-grained potentials based on graph neural networks be interpreted in terms of physically meaningful many-body contributions to the total energy?
papers.core_contribution: Extends GNN-LRP to interpret coarse-grained neural network potentials, showing the learned energy can be decomposed into physically meaningful many-body contributions.
papers.conclusion: GNN-LRP provides a way to interpret machine learned coarse-grained potentials, showing the learned interactions are physically meaningful and offering insights into molecular systems.
papers.key_findings:
For methane and water, 2-body relevance scores show repulsive interactions at short distances and, for water, stabilizing interactions at the first solvation shell.
3-body interactions are crucial for water to recover structural properties, with relevance scores indicating stabilizing and destabilizing contributions.
For protein NTL9, relevance scores identify stabilizing interactions in the folded state and can distinguish between two folding pathways.
The method can analyze the effect of mutations by changing bead embeddings, showing the model learns amino-acid specific interactions.
Different GNN architectures (PaiNN and SO3Net) learn similar underlying physical interactions despite different functional representations.
future_direction: Refining the concepts to provide greater insight and systematic choice of architecture and functionalization.
papers.abstract: Machine learned potentials are becoming a popular tool to define an effective energy model for complex systems, either incorporating electronic structure effects at the atomistic resolution, or effectively renormalizing part of the atomistic degrees of freedom at a coarse-grained resolution. One of the main criticisms to machine learned potentials is that the energy inferred by the network is not as interpretable as in more traditional approaches where a simpler functional form is used. Here we address this problem by extending tools recently proposed in the nascent field of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to coarse-grained potentials based on graph neural networks (GNN). We demonstrate the approach on three different coarse-grained systems including two fluids (methane and water) and the protein NTL9. On these examples, we show that the neural network potentials can be in practice decomposed in relevance contributions to different orders, that can be directly interpreted and provide physical insights on the systems of interest.

papers.title: Using deep LSD to build operators in GANs latent space with meaning in real space
papers.research_question: Can we expand the latent space representation of data elements in terms of an orthonormal basis set that maps to labeled features?
papers.core_contribution: A method to build a set of orthogonal vectors (quasi-eigenvectors) in the latent space of a trained GAN that span the latent space and map one-to-one to labeled features in real space, enabling classification, denoising, and feature transformations.
papers.conclusion: It is possible to build orthogonal vectors in latent space that map to labeled features, revealing the latent space topology, and these vectors can be used for denoising and feature transformations.
papers.key_findings:
The quasi-eigenvectors form a basis in latent space and map to specific labeled features.
For MNIST, 98% of the test-set data maps to a small subset of latent space dimensions (the first 4 quasi-eigenvectors).
The LSD method can be used for classification with 92% accuracy.
The LSD method can denoise images by truncating the expansion to a few quasi-eigenvectors.
Rotation operators in latent space built from quasi-eigenvectors can transform features in real space (e.g., change digit labels).
papers.limitation:
The method assumes labeled data, which is difficult to obtain in real problems.
The method is tested only on MNIST as a proof of concept.
future_direction: Testing the method on broader datasets (CIFAR, ImageNet).
Testing with different latent space dimensionalities and the effect on feature entanglement.
Simplifying the framework (e.g., removing the need for a classifier and encoder).
papers.abstract: Generative models rely on the idea that data can be represented in terms of latent variables which are uncorrelated by definition. Lack of correlation among the latent variable support is important because it suggests that the latent-space manifold is simpler to understand and manipulate than the real-space representation. Many types of generative model are used in deep learning, e.g., variational autoencoders (VAEs) and generative adversarial networks (GANs). Based on the idea that the latent space behaves like a vector space Radford et al. (2015), we ask whether we can expand the latent space representation of our data elements in terms of an orthonormal basis set. Here we propose a method to build a set of linearly independent vectors in the latent space of a trained GAN, which we call quasi-eigenvectors. These quasi-eigenvectors have two key properties: i) They span the latent space, ii) A set of these quasi-eigenvectors map to each of the labeled features one-to-one. We show that in the case of the MNIST image data set, while the number of dimensions in latent space is large by design, 98% of the data in real space map to a sub-domain of latent space of dimensionality equal to the number of labels. We then show how the quasi-eigenvectors can be used for Latent Spectral Decomposition (LSD). We apply LSD to denoise MNIST images. Finally, using the quasi-eigenvectors, we construct rotation matrices in latent space which map to feature transformations in real space. Overall, from quasi-eigenvectors we gain insight regarding the latent space topology.

papers.title: Beyond Interpretability: The Gains of Feature Monosemanticity on Model Robustness
papers.research_question: Does feature monosemanticity, which improves interpretability, also improve model robustness, challenging the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff?
papers.core_contribution: This paper challenges the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff by showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also provide concrete gains in model robustness across various scenarios including noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that monosemanticity offers advantages beyond interpretability, improving model robustness across multiple learning scenarios, and advocates for exploring its broader learning benefits.
papers.key_findings:
Monosemantic features (from NCL or SAE) are more robust than polysemantic features under linear probing with label noise and input noise.
Maintaining monosemanticity during finetuning (via non-negative tuning) reduces overfitting and improves performance in few-shot and noisy-label settings.
MonoLoRA, a sparse variant of LoRA, better preserves alignment safety while maintaining task performance when finetuning LLMs on small datasets.
Empirical analysis shows that classifiers with higher robustness under noise rely more on monosemantic features.
Theoretical analysis on a toy model indicates monosemantic features have better linear separability under noise, leading to more robust decision boundaries.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models often suffer from a lack of interpretability due to polysemanticity, where individual neurons are activated by multiple unrelated semantics, resulting in unclear attributions of model behavior. Recent advances in monosemanticity, where neurons correspond to consistent and distinct semantics, have significantly improved interpretability but are commonly believed to compromise accuracy. In this work, we challenge the prevailing belief of the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff, showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also bring concrete gains in model performance. Across multiple robust learning scenarios-including input and label noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization-our results show that models leveraging monosemantic features significantly outperform those relying on polysemantic features. Furthermore, we provide empirical and theoretical understandings on the robustness gains of feature monosemanticity. Our preliminary analysis suggests that monosemanticity, by promoting better separation of feature representations, leads to more robust decision boundaries. This diverse evidence highlights the generality of monosemanticity in improving model robustness. As a first step in this new direction, we embark on exploring the learning benefits of monosemanticity beyond interpretability, supporting the long-standing hypothesis of linking interpretability and robustness. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/PKU-ML/Beyond_Interpretability}.

papers.title: Interpretability with full complexity by constraining feature information
papers.research_question: How can we achieve interpretability in machine learning without sacrificing model complexity by constraining the information about input features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for interpretability that constrains the information flow from each input feature without restricting model complexity, using the Distributed Information Bottleneck, providing a continuum of feature importance and fine-grained inspection of feature effects.
papers.conclusion: The Distributed Information Bottleneck provides a novel source of interpretability by illuminating where information resides in the input features, without sacrificing model complexity.
papers.key_findings:
The method can identify the features and feature values most important for prediction by analyzing the optimal information allocation.
It allows full complexity of feature processing and interactions, compatible with arbitrary neural network architectures.
It provides a learned continuum of feature inclusion-to-exclusion and fine-grained compression schemes for each feature.
The method is intuitive to implement with minimal additional overhead, training a single model while sweeping the information bottleneck strength.
It demonstrates utility on a range of tabular datasets, providing interpretability signals comparable to or exceeding other methods.
papers.abstract: Interpretability is a pressing issue for machine learning. Common approaches to interpretable machine learning constrain interactions between features of the input, rendering the effects of those features on a model's output comprehensible but at the expense of model complexity. We approach interpretability from a new angle: constrain the information about the features without restricting the complexity of the model. Borrowing from information theory, we use the Distributed Information Bottleneck to find optimal compressions of each feature that maximally preserve information about the output. The learned information allocation, by feature and by feature value, provides rich opportunities for interpretation, particularly in problems with many features and complex feature interactions. The central object of analysis is not a single trained model, but rather a spectrum of models serving as approximations that leverage variable amounts of information about the inputs. Information is allocated to features by their relevance to the output, thereby solving the problem of feature selection by constructing a learned continuum of feature inclusion-to-exclusion. The optimal compression of each feature -- at every stage of approximation -- allows fine-grained inspection of the distinctions among feature values that are most impactful for prediction. We develop a framework for extracting insight from the spectrum of approximate models and demonstrate its utility on a range of tabular datasets.

papers.title: Decomposing Representation Space into Interpretable Subspaces with Unsupervised Learning
papers.research_question: Can we find interpretable subspaces in neural representations in an unsupervised way? To what extent are different aspects organized in separate subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (NDM) to decompose representation space into interpretable subspaces, showing that these subspaces align with known circuit variables and can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Unsupervised decomposition of representation space into interpretable subspaces is possible, and these subspaces can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis, offering a new perspective on understanding model internals.
papers.key_findings:
NDM can find interpretable subspaces without supervision, as shown in toy models and real language models.
Subspaces found by NDM align with variables in known circuits in GPT-2, as evidenced by high Gini coefficients in subspace patching experiments.
The method scales to 2B models, finding separate subspaces for context and parametric knowledge routing.
Qualitative analysis shows that subspaces are consistent and interpretable across different inputs.
papers.limitation: The method can get stuck in local minima, leading to sub-optimal subspace partitions.
future_direction: hierarchical structure of subspaces
more flexible searching over dimension configurations
applying the method to larger models and more tasks
papers.abstract: Understanding internal representations of neural models is a core interest of mechanistic interpretability. Due to its large dimensionality, the representation space can encode various aspects about inputs. To what extent are different aspects organized and encoded in separate subspaces? Is it possible to find these ``natural'' subspaces in a purely unsupervised way? Somewhat surprisingly, we can indeed achieve this and find interpretable subspaces by a seemingly unrelated training objective. Our method, neighbor distance minimization (NDM), learns non-basis-aligned subspaces in an unsupervised manner. Qualitative analysis shows subspaces are interpretable in many cases, and encoded information in obtained subspaces tends to share the same abstract concept across different inputs, making such subspaces similar to ``variables'' used by the model. We also conduct quantitative experiments using known circuits in GPT-2; results show a strong connection between subspaces and circuit variables. We also provide evidence showing scalability to 2B models by finding separate subspaces mediating context and parametric knowledge routing. Viewed more broadly, our findings offer a new perspective on understanding model internals and building circuits.

papers.title: Investigation of Internal Functioning of the Radial-Basis-Function Neural Network River Flow Forecasting Models
papers.research_question: Can hydrological knowledge be extracted from Radial Basis Function Neural Networks (RBFNNs) by interpreting their internal functioning, specifically by examining the responses of hidden layer neurons to understand how they represent flow components in river flow forecasting?
papers.core_contribution: The hidden neurons in an RBFNN for river flow forecasting are not arbitrary but represent specific flow components (baseflow, interflow, surface runoff), demonstrating that hydrological knowledge can be extracted from the model's internal functioning.
papers.conclusion: The RBFNN can be used as an effective flow forecasting tool, and its hidden neurons activate in a way that corresponds to hydrological flow components, suggesting that the network's internal functioning is interpretable and can extract meaningful hydrological knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The RBFNN is an effective tool for daily flow forecasting.
The activation of hidden nodes is not arbitrary; each node dominates in one of the flow domains (low, medium, high) and represents flow components resembling baseflow, interflow, and surface runoff.
The proportional contribution from each hidden neuron varies over time, reflecting dominance in specific flow ranges.
The RBFNN parameters (centers, spreads, weights) function to decompose the flow hydrograph into meaningful components.
The method provides insight into the internal functioning of RBFNNs, showing they can mimic local models corresponding to hydrological processes.
papers.limitation: The study uses a limited number of catchments, so the findings may not generalize to all catchments.
future_direction: Apply the methodology to a large number of catchments with different characteristics.
Investigate the sensitivity of the number of RBFs and network structure to represent physical processes.
papers.abstract: This paper deals with the challenging problem of hydrological interpretation of the internal functioning of artificial neural networks (ANNs) by extracting knowledge from their solutions. The neural network used in this study is based on the structure of the radial-basis-function neural network (RBFNN), which is considered as an alternative to the multilayer perceptron for solving complex modeling problems. This network consists of input, hidden, and output layers. The network is trained using the daily data of two catchments having different characteristics and from two different regions in the world. The present day and antecedent observed discharges are used as inputs to the network to forecast the flow one day ahead. A range of quantitative and qualitative techniques are used for hydrological interpretation of the internal functioning by examining the responses of the hidden layer nodes. The results of the study show that a single hidden layered RBFNN is an effective tool to forecast the daily flows and that the activation of the hidden layer nodes are far from arbitrary, but appear to represent flow components of the predicted hydrograph. The results of the study confirm that the three nodes in the hidden layer of this model effectively divide the input data space in such a way that the contribution from each node dominates in one of the flow domains—low, medium, or high—and form, in a crude manner, the base flow, interflow and surface runoff components of the hydrograph.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn Visual Concepts in Histopathology
papers.research_question: Can self-supervised learning, particularly DINO-based knowledge distillation, learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images?
papers.core_contribution: Vision Transformers using DINO-based self-supervised learning learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images, with different attention heads capturing distinct morphological phenotypes.
papers.conclusion: Self-supervised learning, particularly DINO, is effective for learning representations in histopathology, and the attention heads of Vision Transformers provide interpretable visual concepts that can aid in biomarker discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 features are a strong baseline, achieving comparable performance to self-supervised methods on many tasks.
Self-supervised features, particularly from DINO, are robust and sample-efficient, performing well with less training data.
DINO outperforms SimCLR on weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks in histopathology.
DINO's attention heads learn distinct morphological visual concepts, localizing cells, stroma tissue, and fat/air pockets.
papers.limitation: Performance benefit of self-supervised learning may vary depending on organ type (only breast tissue tested) and weakly-supervised architecture (only CLAM tested).
future_direction: Assess the utility of self-supervised methods for learning representations of histopathological images from rare diseases with data paucity of slide-level and patch-level annotations.
papers.abstract: Tissue phenotyping is a fundamental task in learning objective characterizations of histopathologic biomarkers within the tumor-immune microenvironment in cancer pathology. However, whole-slide imaging (WSI) is a complex computer vision in which: 1) WSIs have enormous image resolutions with precludes large-scale pixel-level efforts in data curation, and 2) diversity of morphological phenotypes results in inter- and intra-observer variability in tissue labeling. To address these limitations, current efforts have proposed using pretrained image encoders (transfer learning from ImageNet, self-supervised pretraining) in extracting morphological features from pathology, but have not been extensively validated. In this work, we conduct a search for good representations in pathology by training a variety of self-supervised models with validation on a variety of weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks. Our key finding is in discovering that Vision Transformers using DINO-based knowledge distillation are able to learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images wherein the different attention heads learn distinct morphological phenotypes. We make evaluation code and pretrained weights publicly-available at: https://github.com/Richarizardd/Self-Supervised-ViT-Path.

papers.title: Enhancing Interpretability of Sparse Latent Representations with Class Information
papers.research_question: How can latent space interpretability be enhanced by ensuring that active dimensions in the latent space are consistent across samples within the same class, thereby capturing both global and class-specific factors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel loss function for Variational Sparse Coding that aligns active latent dimensions across samples within the same class, enhancing interpretability by capturing both global and class-specific factors in the latent space.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method enhances latent space interpretability by capturing both global and class-specific features, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the latent space, especially in datasets where global attributes are not uniformly present.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method successfully aligns active latent dimensions within each class, creating a more structured and interpretable latent space.
The method captures global features (e.g., digit thickness and rotation in MNIST) that are shared across all classes.
The method also captures class-specific features (e.g., intersection point in digits 4 and 9, heel prominence in footwear classes in Fashion-MNIST).
Classes within the same category (e.g., boots, sandals, sneakers) share more common active dimensions, indicating stronger latent similarities.
Quantitative analysis using distance metrics (Pearson correlation, Cosine, Euclidean) confirms higher similarity between gamma vectors of classes within the same category.
papers.abstract: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are powerful generative models for learning latent representations. Standard VAEs generate dispersed and unstructured latent spaces by utilizing all dimensions, which limits their interpretability, especially in high-dimensional spaces. To address this challenge, Variational Sparse Coding (VSC) introduces a spike-and-slab prior distribution, resulting in sparse latent representations for each input. These sparse representations, characterized by a limited number of active dimensions, are inherently more interpretable. Despite this advantage, VSC falls short in providing structured interpretations across samples within the same class. Intuitively, samples from the same class are expected to share similar attributes while allowing for variations in those attributes. This expectation should manifest as consistent patterns of active dimensions in their latent representations, but VSC does not enforce such consistency. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to enhance the latent space interpretability by ensuring that the active dimensions in the latent space are consistent across samples within the same class. To achieve this, we introduce a new loss function that encourages samples from the same class to share similar active dimensions. This alignment creates a more structured and interpretable latent space, where each shared dimension corresponds to a high-level concept, or "factor." Unlike existing disentanglement-based methods that primarily focus on global factors shared across all classes, our method captures both global and class-specific factors, thereby enhancing the utility and interpretability of latent representations.

papers.title: DeepMiner: Discovering Interpretable Representations for Mammogram Classification and Explanation
papers.research_question: How to discover interpretable representations in deep neural networks and build explanations for medical predictions, specifically for mammogram classification.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DeepMiner, a human-in-the-loop framework for discovering interpretable representations in CNNs and generating explanations for medical predictions, specifically for mammogram classification.
papers.conclusion: DeepMiner is a framework that uncovers interpretable representations in deep neural networks and builds explanations for deep network predictions, and it is applicable to many other domains.
papers.key_findings:
Many individual units in the final convolutional layer of a CNN respond strongly to diseased tissue concepts specified by the BI-RADS lexicon.
DeepMiner can generate explanations for CNN mammogram classification that are consistent with ground truth radiology reports.
DeepMiner enables better understanding of the nuances of CNN classification decisions and possibly discovers new visual knowledge relevant to medical diagnosis.
future_direction: Generalization to other medical image classification tasks.
Incorporation of auxiliary features such as genetic information.
Potential for discovering unknown discriminative visual features for diseases less well understood than breast cancer.
papers.abstract: We propose DeepMiner, a framework to discover interpretable representations in deep neural networks and to build explanations for medical predictions. By probing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained to classify cancer in mammograms, we show that many individual units in the final convolutional layer of a CNN respond strongly to diseased tissue concepts specified by the Breast Imaging-Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) lexicon. After expert annotation of the interpretable units, our proposed method is able to generate explanations for CNN mammogram classification that are consistent with ground truth radiology reports on the Digital Database for Screening Mammography. We show that DeepMiner not only enables better understanding of the nuances of CNN classification decisions but also possibly discovers new visual knowledge relevant to medical diagnosis.

papers.title: Amortized Spectral Kernel Discovery via Prior-Data Fitted Network
papers.research_question: How can we extract explicit spectral densities and stationary kernels from pre-trained Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) to improve interpretability and enable downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interpretability framework and decoder architectures to extract explicit spectral density estimates and corresponding stationary kernels from the latent representations of frozen Prior-Data Fitted Networks, enabling amortized kernel discovery without iterative optimization.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that PFNs implicitly encode structured spectral information, which can be decoded into explicit, portable kernel representations, bridging the gap between amortized inference and interpretable kernel discovery for scientific and downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic analysis shows the attention latent output (H) in PFNs encodes the spectral content of the input function, forming a smooth manifold correlated with frequency.
The proposed Filter Bank Decoder can recover complex multi-peak spectral mixtures and construct explicit stationary kernels via Bochner's theorem.
Decoded kernels achieve Gaussian process regression performance comparable to the original PFN and optimization-based baselines (Deep Kernel Learning, Random Fourier Features) while requiring only a single forward pass, yielding orders-of-magnitude inference speedups.
Theoretical analysis characterizes the identifiability limits of spectral density: spectral weights are non-identifiable from a single normalized realization but become identifiable with multiple independent realizations.
The framework operates effectively in both single-realization and multi-realization regimes, with an analytical scaling module to resolve global scale ambiguity in the single-function setting.
papers.limitation:
The decoded kernels are explicit stationary surrogate kernels obtained via Bochner's theorem; they are not exact reconstructions of the PFN's internal attention mechanism nor guaranteed to match the true data-generating GP kernel.
In the single-realization setting, spectral weights are not identifiable from a single normalized function sample, limiting full spectral recovery.
papers.abstract: Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) enable efficient amortized inference but lack transparent access to their learned priors and kernels. This opacity hinders their use in downstream tasks, such as surrogate-based optimization, that require explicit covariance models. We introduce an interpretability-driven framework for amortized spectral discovery from pre-trained PFNs with decoupled attention. We perform a mechanistic analysis on a trained PFN that identifies attention latent output as the key intermediary, linking observed function data to spectral structure. Building on this insight, we propose decoder architectures that map PFN latents to explicit spectral density estimates and corresponding stationary kernels via Bochner's theorem. We study this pipeline in both single-realization and multi-realization regimes, contextualizing theoretical limits on spectral identifiability and proving consistency when multiple function samples are available. Empirically, the proposed decoders recover complex multi-peak spectral mixtures and produce explicit kernels that support Gaussian process regression with accuracy comparable to PFNs and optimization-based baselines, while requiring only a single forward pass. This yields orders-of-magnitude reductions in inference time compared to optimization-based baselines.

papers.title: Understanding the Latent Space of Diffusion Models through the Lens of Riemannian Geometry
papers.research_question: How can we understand the latent space of diffusion models from a geometrical perspective, and how does this structure evolve during the generative process and with text conditions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a geometric analysis of the latent space of diffusion models using the pullback metric, enabling unsupervised image editing via latent basis traversal and providing insights into how the latent structure evolves during generation and with text conditions.
papers.conclusion: The geometric analysis of diffusion models' latent space using the pullback metric provides a deeper understanding and opens new possibilities for adopting diffusion models in useful applications.
papers.key_findings:
The discovered local latent basis enables semantic image editing by moving the latent variable xt along the basis vector at a specific timestep.
The geometric structure of the latent space evolves from low-frequency to high-frequency components during the generative process, confirming coarse-to-fine generation.
The discrepancy between tangent spaces of different samples increases along the generative process, making generally applicable editing directions harder to find later.
Diffusion models trained on simpler datasets (e.g., CelebA-HQ) exhibit more consistent tangent spaces across timesteps compared to complex datasets (e.g., ImageNet).
Similar text prompts yield similar tangent spaces, and the influence of the prompt on the tangent space becomes weaker in later timesteps.
papers.limitation:
Entanglement of semantic directions due to dataset biases (e.g., beard editing converting female to male).
Occasional abrupt changes during editing in Stable Diffusion, highlighting the complex geometry of the latent space.
The method assumes the feature space H has a Euclidean metric, which may not hold for other architectural designs.
future_direction: Exploring the reasons behind the effectiveness of x-space guidance.
Investigating the disentanglement capability of the latent space X compared to the feature space H.
Analyzing the latent space of other architectural designs, such as transformer-based diffusion models.
papers.abstract: Despite the success of diffusion models (DMs), we still lack a thorough understanding of their latent space. To understand the latent space $\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathcal{X}$, we analyze them from a geometrical perspective. Our approach involves deriving the local latent basis within $\mathcal{X}$ by leveraging the pullback metric associated with their encoding feature maps. Remarkably, our discovered local latent basis enables image editing capabilities by moving $\mathbf{x}_t$, the latent space of DMs, along the basis vector at specific timesteps. We further analyze how the geometric structure of DMs evolves over diffusion timesteps and differs across different text conditions. This confirms the known phenomenon of coarse-to-fine generation, as well as reveals novel insights such as the discrepancy between $\mathbf{x}_t$ across timesteps, the effect of dataset complexity, and the time-varying influence of text prompts. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first to present image editing through $\mathbf{x}$-space traversal, editing only once at specific timestep $t$ without any additional training, and providing thorough analyses of the latent structure of DMs. The code to reproduce our experiments can be found at https://github.com/enkeejunior1/Diffusion-Pullback.

papers.title: Neural network interpretation using descrambler groups
papers.research_question: How can inner layer signalling of fully connected neural networks be brought into a human-readable form to improve interpretability, particularly in digital signal processing and scientific computing?
papers.core_contribution: A group-theoretical method (descrambler groups) for interpreting fully connected neural networks by finding orthogonal transformations that make intermediate signals human-readable, successfully revealing sophisticated signal processing operations in a DSP network.
papers.conclusion: The descrambler group method enables interpretation of fully connected neural networks, revealing that even small networks can invent complex mathematical operations, and that reductionist understanding is possible.
papers.key_findings:
The descrambler group method can successfully interpret the inner workings of fully connected neural networks.
DEERNet spontaneously invents a bandpass filter, a notch filter, a frequency axis rectifier, frequency division multiplexing, spectral filtering regularization, and a Fourier-like transform mapping harmonics to Chebyshev polynomials.
The method reveals that even small networks can develop complex, interpretable mathematical operations during training.
The descrambling process requires defining a problem-specific interpretability metric, such as signal smoothness or diagonal dominance.
The method is applicable to fully connected layers, which are harder to interpret than convolutional layers.
papers.limitation: The method requires domain-specific expertise to recognize the functionality of descrambled weight matrices, and the descrambled matrix may still be uninterpretable to non-specialists.
future_direction: Neural networks can be mined for new knowledge, possibly discovering previously unknown mathematics.
A staged approach is recommended: first establish the role of each layer empirically, then descramble for implementation details.
papers.abstract: The lack of interpretability and trust is a much-criticized feature of deep neural networks. In fully connected nets, the signaling between inner layers is scrambled because backpropagation training does not require perceptrons to be arranged in any particular order. The result is a black box; this problem is particularly severe in scientific computing and digital signal processing (DSP), where neural nets perform abstract mathematical transformations that do not reduce to features or concepts. We present here a group-theoretical procedure that attempts to bring inner-layer signaling into a human-readable form, the assumption being that this form exists and has identifiable and quantifiable features-for example, smoothness or locality. We applied the proposed method to DEERNet (a DSP network used in electron spin resonance) and managed to descramble it. We found considerable internal sophistication: the network spontaneously invents a bandpass filter, a notch filter, a frequency axis rescaling transformation, frequency-division multiplexing, group embedding, spectral filtering regularization, and a map from harmonic functions into Chebyshev polynomials-in 10 min of unattended training from a random initial guess.

papers.title: ProtSAE: Disentangling and Interpreting Protein Language Models via Semantically-Guided Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle semantic features in protein language models to improve interpretability and enable precise model control?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ProtSAE, a semantically-guided sparse autoencoder that disentangles protein features and aligns them with biological concepts, improving interpretability and enabling steering of protein language models.
papers.conclusion: ProtSAE effectively disentangles semantic features in protein language models, leading to better interpretability and control for protein engineering tasks.
papers.key_findings:
ProtSAE learns more biologically relevant and interpretable hidden features compared to previous SAE methods.
ProtSAE maintains high reconstruction fidelity while achieving better results in interpretable probing.
ProtSAE enables effective steering of PLM outputs for downstream generation tasks.
Ablation studies show that the semantic guidance components (annotation data and domain knowledge) are crucial for performance.
papers.limitation: ProtSAE is only evaluated on ESM2 and not scaled to broader architectures or application scenarios.
future_direction: Extend ProtSAE to protein language models aligned with natural language.
Apply ProtSAE to sequence-structure co-design models.
Explore interpretable feature extraction from protein structure prediction models and generative diffusion models.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) has emerged as a powerful tool for mechanistic interpretability of large language models. Recent works apply SAE to protein language models (PLMs), aiming to extract and analyze biologically meaningful features from their latent spaces. However, SAE suffers from semantic entanglement, where individual neurons often mix multiple nonlinear concepts, making it difficult to reliably interpret or manipulate model behaviors. In this paper, we propose a semantically-guided SAE, called ProtSAE. Unlike existing SAE which requires annotation datasets to filter and interpret activations, we guide semantic disentanglement during training using both annotation datasets and domain knowledge to mitigate the effects of entangled attributes. We design interpretability experiments showing that ProtSAE learns more biologically relevant and interpretable hidden features compared to previous methods. Performance analyses further demonstrate that ProtSAE maintains high reconstruction fidelity while achieving better results in interpretable probing. We also show the potential of ProtSAE in steering PLMs for downstream generation tasks.

papers.title: Studying Limits of Explainability by Integrated Gradients for Gene Expression Models
papers.research_question: What is the relevance of biomarkers identified by Integrated Gradients for gene expression models, and is feature ranking sufficient for robust biomarker identification?
