papers.core_contribution: Proposes metrics (PGU and PGI) and a simulation framework based on LDA to evaluate the robustness of biomarkers identified by Integrated Gradients in gene expression models, highlighting the need for mesoscopic explanations.
papers.conclusion: The study underscores the complexity of gene expression data and the need for careful evaluation of explainability methods, proposing diffusion of attribution scores as a promising approach for better biomarker identification.
papers.key_findings:
Ranking features by importance alone is insufficient for robust biomarker identification; features must be both sufficient and necessary.
On TCGA data, 50 genes are sufficient for classification, but removing them does not degrade performance, indicating redundancy.
Random subsets of 800 genes can achieve good classification accuracy, even excluding important genes.
In simulated data, diffusing IG scores on correlation graphs significantly improves feature agreement, highlighting the importance of considering gene correlations.
papers.limitation: Simulated data is simpler than real biological data, which may limit generalizability.
future_direction: Investigating the diffusion of IG scores on correlation matrices for better explainability.
papers.abstract: Understanding the molecular processes that drive cellular life is a fundamental question in biological research. Ambitious programs have gathered a number of molecular datasets on large populations. To decipher the complex cellular interactions, recent work has turned to supervised machine learning methods. The scientific questions are formulated as classical learning problems on tabular data or on graphs, e.g. phenotype prediction from gene expression data. In these works, the input features on which the individual predictions are predominantly based are often interpreted as indicative of the cause of the phenotype, such as cancer identification. Here, we propose to explore the relevance of the biomarkers identified by Integrated Gradients, an explainability method for feature attribution in machine learning. Through a motivating example on The Cancer Genome Atlas, we show that ranking features by importance is not enough to robustly identify biomarkers. As it is difficult to evaluate whether biomarkers reflect relevant causes without known ground truth, we simulate gene expression data by proposing a hierarchical model based on Latent Dirichlet Allocation models. We also highlight good practices for evaluating explanations for genomics data and propose a direction to derive more insights from these explanations.

papers.title: Neural Networks Trained to Solve Differential Equations Learn General Representations
papers.research_question: How can we measure the generality of neural network layers across a continuously-parametrized set of tasks? What is the generality structure of layers in neural networks trained to solve differential equations?
papers.core_contribution: We develop an efficient method using SVCCA to measure layer generality across continuously-parametrized tasks, and apply it to show that in neural networks trained to solve differential equations, the first layer is general and deeper layers are successively more specific.
papers.conclusion: We presented a method for measuring layer generality using SVCCA, found that first layers of DENNs are general and deeper layers are more specific, validated with transfer learning, and visualized the general components as generalized coordinates.
papers.key_findings:
The first hidden layer is general, and deeper layers become progressively more specific.
The SVCCA-based method agrees with transfer learning experiments but is much faster, especially for continuously-parametrized problems.
The general components of the first layer can be visualized as generalized coordinates that capture regions of interest in the input domain.
Network width affects layer generality: intrinsic dimensionality saturates with width, reproducibility increases with width, and specificity varies with width and layer depth.
Very wide networks may have training dynamics that affect convergence and generality measurements.
papers.limitation:
SVCCA is numerically unstable when correlation values are very close to each other, making component sorting ill-conditioned.
Very wide networks may have broad minima in the loss landscape, causing training to terminate before optimal convergence, potentially affecting generality measurements.
future_direction: Explore the behavior of layer generality at very large network widths.
Develop component analyses that search for closely-coupled components to improve numerical stability.
Investigate different training protocols for very wide DENNs to ensure proper convergence.
papers.abstract: We introduce a technique based on the singular vector canonical correlation analysis (SVCCA) for measuring the generality of neural network layers across a continuously-parametrized set of tasks. We illustrate this method by studying generality in neural networks trained to solve parametrized boundary value problems based on the Poisson partial differential equation. We find that the first hidden layer is general, and that deeper layers are successively more specific. Next, we validate our method against an existing technique that measures layer generality using transfer learning experiments. We find excellent agreement between the two methods, and note that our method is much faster, particularly for continuously-parametrized problems. Finally, we visualize the general representations of the first layers, and interpret them as generalized coordinates over the input domain.

papers.title: Projective Kolmogorov Arnold Neural Networks (P-KANs): Entropy-Driven Functional Space Discovery for Interpretable Machine Learning
papers.research_question: How can we improve Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) by reducing redundancy in spline parameter spaces and guiding edge functions towards interpretable functional representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces P-KANs, a training framework that uses entropy-driven functional space projection to reduce parameter redundancy and improve interpretability in KANs.
papers.conclusion: P-KANs represent a step towards neural architectures that discover mathematical structure, improving parameter efficiency, noise robustness, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
P-KANs achieve up to 80% parameter reduction while maintaining representational capacity.
P-KANs show significantly improved robustness to noise compared to standard KANs.
P-KANs successfully apply to industrial automated fiber placement prediction with minimal data.
papers.limitation:
Computational overhead due to projection operations across multiple functional spaces.
Restriction to classical orthonormal bases may be insufficient for exotic phenomena.
Amplitude scaling issues may limit quantitative accuracy.
Hyperparameter sensitivity complicates deployment.
future_direction: Extending the framework to more general mathematical structures such as differential operators.
Hybrid deployment strategies to balance computational costs and robustness.
papers.abstract: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) relocate learnable nonlinearities from nodes to edges, demonstrating remarkable capabilities in scientific machine learning and interpretable modeling. However, current KAN implementations suffer from fundamental inefficiencies due to redundancy in high-dimensional spline parameter spaces, where numerous distinct parameterisations yield functionally equivalent behaviors. This redundancy manifests as a "nuisance space" in the model's Jacobian, leading to susceptibility to overfitting and poor generalization. We introduce Projective Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (P-KANs), a novel training framework that guides edge function discovery towards interpretable functional representations through entropy-minimisation techniques from signal analysis and sparse dictionary learning. Rather than constraining functions to predetermined spaces, our approach maintains spline space flexibility while introducing "gravitational" terms that encourage convergence towards optimal functional representations. Our key insight recognizes that optimal representations can be identified through entropy analysis of projection coefficients, compressing edge functions to lower-parameter projective spaces (Fourier, Chebyshev, Bessel). P-KANs demonstrate superior performance across multiple domains, achieving up to 80% parameter reduction while maintaining representational capacity, significantly improved robustness to noise compared to standard KANs, and successful application to industrial automated fiber placement prediction. Our approach enables automatic discovery of mixed functional representations where different edges converge to different optimal spaces, providing both compression benefits and enhanced interpretability for scientific machine learning applications.

papers.title: Resurrecting the Salmon: Rethinking Mechanistic Interpretability with Domain-Specific Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improve reconstruction fidelity and interpretability compared to broad-domain SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improves reconstruction fidelity, interpretability, and reduces linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggests the field may need to question 'foundation-model' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Domain-specific SAEs achieve 15-20% higher fraction of variance explained and better loss recovery than broad-domain SAEs.
Domain-specific SAEs produce features that are more interpretable and aligned with clinically meaningful concepts.
Domain-specific SAEs capture more linear structure, leaving a smaller and more nonlinear residual error (less dark matter).
Domain-specific SAEs show improved cosine similarity between activations and reconstructions.
Domain-specific SAEs have minimal shrinkage (relative reconstruction bias close to 1).
future_direction: Extending domain-specific SAEs to other specialised domains, such as legal or financial text.
Investigating how domain confinement affects feature splitting and absorption.
Studying the trade-offs between domain breadth and SAE performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose large language model (LLM) activations into latent features that reveal mechanistic structure. Conventional SAEs train on broad data distributions, forcing a fixed latent budget to capture only high-frequency, generic patterns. This often results in significant linear ``dark matter'' in reconstruction error and produces latents that fragment or absorb each other, complicating interpretation. We show that restricting SAE training to a well-defined domain (medical text) reallocates capacity to domain-specific features, improving both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability. Training JumpReLU SAEs on layer-20 activations of Gemma-2 models using 195k clinical QA examples, we find that domain-confined SAEs explain up to 20\% more variance, achieve higher loss recovery, and reduce linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs. Automated and human evaluations confirm that learned features align with clinically meaningful concepts (e.g., ``taste sensations'' or ``infectious mononucleosis''), rather than frequent but uninformative tokens. These domain-specific SAEs capture relevant linear structure, leaving a smaller, more purely nonlinear residual. We conclude that domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggesting the field may need to question ``foundation-model'' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.

papers.title: Learning Policy Representations for Steerable Behavior Synthesis
papers.research_question: How to learn policy representations that enable test-time behavior synthesis via gradient-based optimization in a structured latent space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a policy representation model that learns a smooth and value-aligned latent space, enabling test-time behavior synthesis through gradient-based optimization without additional training.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a principled framework for learning general-purpose policy representations that are smooth and value-aligned, enabling test-time behavior synthesis under unseen constraints through latent space optimization.
papers.key_findings:
The model can reconstruct policies from latent representations with low relative difference in returns.
The latent space exhibits a geometry aligned with value functions, unlike VAEs alone.
The method enables zero-shot behavior synthesis under constraints via latent space optimization.
Projected gradient descent is necessary to keep optimizations on the data manifold.
The method outperforms baselines like VAE and MLP mean-pool in predicting returns.
future_direction: Utilizing the latent space to facilitate online RL exploration and exploitation.
Developing dynamics-augmented latent-conditioned decoders for meta-learning across varying environments.
papers.abstract: Given a Markov decision process (MDP), we seek to learn representations for a range of policies to facilitate behavior steering at test time. As policies of an MDP are uniquely determined by their occupancy measures, we propose modeling policy representations as expectations of state-action feature maps with respect to occupancy measures. We show that these representations can be approximated uniformly for a range of policies using a set-based architecture. Our model encodes a set of state-action samples into a latent embedding, from which we decode both the policy and its value functions corresponding to multiple rewards. We use variational generative approach to induce a smooth latent space, and further shape it with contrastive learning so that latent distances align with differences in value functions. This geometry permits gradient-based optimization directly in the latent space. Leveraging this capability, we solve a novel behavior synthesis task, where policies are steered to satisfy previously unseen value function constraints without additional training.

papers.title: Moments of Clarity: Streamlining Latent Spaces in Machine Learning using Moment Pooling
papers.research_question: How can we reduce the latent space dimensionality of Deep Sets networks while maintaining or improving performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Moment Pooling, a generalization of Deep Sets that uses multivariate moments to drastically reduce the required latent dimension while maintaining performance, enabling direct visualization and closed-form extraction of learned representations.
papers.conclusion: Moment Pooling is an effective method for reducing latent space dimensionality in Deep Sets architectures, improving interpretability and enabling the extraction of closed-form observables, as demonstrated in collider physics jet classification tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Moment EFNs with very small latent dimensions (e.g., L=1) achieve performance comparable to ordinary EFNs with higher latent dimensions on quark/gluon jet classification.
The latent space of small-L Moment EFNs can be visualized and fit to simple closed-form expressions, such as 'log angularities'.
For quark/gluon discrimination, model performance correlates strongly with the effective latent dimension Leff, indicating the task is compressible via moments.
The method allows for the extraction of analytic observables from the trained model, though finding closed forms for the F network beyond k=2 is nontrivial.
Not all tasks are equally compressible; top/QCD discrimination does not show the same performance gains per effective latent dimension.
papers.limitation:
Not all observables can be efficiently compressed with Moment Pooling; for example, top/QCD jet discrimination does not show the same compressibility as quark/gluon discrimination.
Finding closed-form expressions for the F network (the decoder) becomes difficult for higher-order moments (k > 2).
future_direction: Extending Moment Pooling to other architectures, such as transformers.
Exploring the use of cumulants instead of moments (Cumulant Pooling).
Applying the method to other tasks beyond jet classification.
papers.abstract: Many machine learning applications involve learning a latent representation of data, which is often high-dimensional and difficult to directly interpret. In this work, we propose "Moment Pooling", a natural extension of Deep Sets networks which drastically decrease latent space dimensionality of these networks while maintaining or even improving performance. Moment Pooling generalizes the summation in Deep Sets to arbitrary multivariate moments, which enables the model to achieve a much higher effective latent dimensionality for a fixed latent dimension. We demonstrate Moment Pooling on the collider physics task of quark/gluon jet classification by extending Energy Flow Networks (EFNs) to Moment EFNs. We find that Moment EFNs with latent dimensions as small as 1 perform similarly to ordinary EFNs with higher latent dimension. This small latent dimension allows for the internal representation to be directly visualized and interpreted, which in turn enables the learned internal jet representation to be extracted in closed form.

papers.title: Maximum entropy methods for extracting the learned features of deep neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we interpret deep neural networks and extract the features they learn from input data using maximum entropy methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a maximum entropy method for interpreting deep neural networks by sampling sequences that preserve penultimate layer activations, allowing extraction of learned features such as motifs and nucleosome positioning signals.
papers.conclusion: The maximum entropy method provides a valuable tool for interpreting deep neural networks, particularly in biological sequence analysis, and demonstrates synergy between statistical physics and machine learning for extracting subtle sequence features.
papers.key_findings:
The MaxEnt method successfully captures XOR logic learned by a simple ANN, while Saliency Map and DeepLIFT methods fail to do so.
The MaxEnt method localizes CTCF binding motifs with better agreement with conventional motif discovery tools (MEME/FIMO) than Saliency Map and DeepLIFT.
The MaxEnt method extracts nucleosome positioning signals, including periodic GC content at 10 bp intervals, more effectively than Saliency Map and DeepLIFT.
The method can assess the importance of global sequence features (e.g., GC content) via a feature importance score derived from the variance of MCMC samples.
Features extracted by MaxEnt (low-variance principal components) can be used for classification, as demonstrated by a nearest neighbor classifier achieving 76% accuracy.
papers.limitation: The MaxEnt method is computationally expensive compared to Saliency Map and DeepLIFT due to MCMC sampling.
papers.abstract: New architectures of multilayer artificial neural networks and new methods for training them are rapidly revolutionizing the application of machine learning in diverse fields, including business, social science, physical sciences, and biology. Interpreting deep neural networks, however, currently remains elusive, and a critical challenge lies in understanding which meaningful features a network is actually learning. We present a general method for interpreting deep neural networks and extracting network-learned features from input data. We describe our algorithm in the context of biological sequence analysis. Our approach, based on ideas from statistical physics, samples from the maximum entropy distribution over possible sequences, anchored at an input sequence and subject to constraints implied by the empirical function learned by a network. Using our framework, we demonstrate that local transcription factor binding motifs can be identified from a network trained on ChIP-seq data and that nucleosome positioning signals are indeed learned by a network trained on chemical cleavage nucleosome maps. Imposing a further constraint on the maximum entropy distribution also allows us to probe whether a network is learning global sequence features, such as the high GC content in nucleosome-rich regions. This work thus provides valuable mathematical tools for interpreting and extracting learned features from feed-forward neural networks.

papers.title: BERT Learns (and Teaches) Chemistry
papers.research_question: Can attention mechanisms in BERT be used to identify important molecular substructures (functional groups) from SMILES string representations and apply these learned representations to chemical property prediction tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that BERT's attention mechanisms can identify chemically relevant functional groups from SMILES strings without domain heuristics, and that these learned representations can be applied to downstream chemical property prediction tasks.
papers.conclusion: Attention visualization in BERT provides a data-driven method to identify functional groups and important molecular substructures from SMILES strings, offering a potentially useful tool for computational chemistry despite not achieving state-of-the-art performance on downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's attention heads, trained only on SMILES strings, learn to attend to atoms that correspond to known active reaction sites (functional groups) in molecules, even without explicit reaction data.
When fine-tuned on chemical property regression tasks (e.g., solubility), specific attention heads in BERT focus on relevant substructures (e.g., carbon chains for solubility).
Using BERT embeddings as features for graph models (GCN, GAT) on toxicity prediction tasks yields competitive but not state-of-the-art performance compared to canonical atom featurization.
Attention visualization of BERT trained on chemical data can serve as a tool for chemistry practitioners to quickly identify important substructures related to various chemical properties.
papers.limitation:
BERT embeddings did not improve upon the state of the art when used as features for graph models on toxicity prediction; the learned information appears to be a subset of that captured by canonical atom featurization.
Some molecules in the Tox21 dataset contain atoms not present in BERT's vocabulary, which may detract from performance.
Attention heads after fine-tuning on most chemical property tasks (QED, SAS) showed little change from pretraining, except for the solubility task, suggesting the fine-tuning may find a local optimum close to pretraining weights.
future_direction: Using a larger dataset of 96 million molecules from PubMed to train BERT, given that language models thrive with abundant data.
Designing a loss function that penalizes distances between embeddings of different SMILES strings representing the same molecule to force BERT to learn the inherent graphical meaning.
Further investigating the approach of analyzing chemical property-bearing molecular substructures via fine-tuning to make it a more useful tool for chemists.
papers.abstract: Modern computational organic chemistry is becoming increasingly data-driven. There remain a large number of important unsolved problems in this area such as product prediction given reactants, drug discovery, and metric-optimized molecule synthesis, but efforts to solve these problems using machine learning have also increased in recent years. In this work, we propose the use of attention to study functional groups and other property-impacting molecular substructures from a data-driven perspective, using a transformer-based model (BERT) on datasets of string representations of molecules and analyzing the behavior of its attention heads. We then apply the representations of functional groups and atoms learned by the model to tackle problems of toxicity, solubility, drug-likeness, and synthesis accessibility on smaller datasets using the learned representations as features for graph convolution and attention models on the graph structure of molecules, as well as fine-tuning of BERT. Finally, we propose the use of attention visualization as a helpful tool for chemistry practitioners and students to quickly identify important substructures in various chemical properties.

papers.title: DGTN: Graph-Enhanced Transformer with Diffusive Attention Gating Mechanism for Enzyme DDG Prediction
papers.research_question: How can we accurately predict the effect of amino acid mutations on enzyme thermodynamic stability (∆∆G) by integrating sequence and structural information through a co-learning framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DGTN, a novel architecture that co-learns graph neural network and transformer representations through a bidirectional diffusion mechanism for protein stability prediction, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
papers.conclusion: DGTN effectively integrates 3D geometric and evolutionary sequence context through bidirectional diffusion, establishing a principled and interpretable paradigm for accurate protein stability prediction and design.
papers.key_findings:
DGTN achieves state-of-the-art performance on ProTherm with Pearson correlation ρ=0.87 and RMSE=1.21 kcal/mol, outperforming existing baselines.
Ablation studies show the bidirectional diffusion mechanism contributes a 6-point gain in Pearson correlation over simple cross-modal fusion.
The model generalizes well to unseen datasets (SKEMPI, Ssym, FireProtDB), demonstrating robust learning of stability principles.
Theoretical analysis proves the diffused attention converges to an optimal structure-aware attention matrix with a convergence rate of O(1/√T).
Attention visualization confirms the model successfully identifies spatially proximate but sequentially distant residue interactions.
papers.limitation:
Operates on a single static conformation of the wild-type protein, unable to capture dynamic or entropic contributions to stability.
Evaluates mutations in isolation and does not explicitly model epistatic (non-additive) interactions between multiple substitutions.
Training data (ProTherm) exhibits class imbalance, with certain protein families overrepresented, potentially limiting generalization.
future_direction: Incorporate ensembles of structures (from molecular dynamics or predicted distributions) to model flexibility and allostery.
Extend the architecture to jointly represent combinatorial mutations via graph-based mutation encoding or interaction-aware attention.
Improve robustness to dataset imbalance via domain-adversarial training, balanced sampling, or cross-family transfer learning.
papers.abstract: Predicting the effect of amino acid mutations on enzyme thermodynamic stability (DDG) is fundamental to protein engineering and drug design. While recent deep learning approaches have shown promise, they often process sequence and structure information independently, failing to capture the intricate coupling between local structural geometry and global sequential patterns. We present DGTN (Diffused Graph-Transformer Network), a novel architecture that co-learns graph neural network (GNN) weights for structural priors and transformer attention through a diffusion mechanism. Our key innovation is a bidirectional diffusion process where: (1) GNN-derived structural embeddings guide transformer attention via learnable diffusion kernels, and (2) transformer representations refine GNN message passing through attention-modulated graph updates. We provide rigorous mathematical analysis showing this co-learning scheme achieves provably better approximation bounds than independent processing. On ProTherm and SKEMPI benchmarks, DGTN achieves state-of-the-art performance (Pearson Rho = 0.87, RMSE = 1.21 kcal/mol), with 6.2% improvement over best baselines. Ablation studies confirm the diffusion mechanism contributes 4.8 points to correlation. Our theoretical analysis proves the diffused attention converges to optimal structure-sequence coupling, with convergence rate O(1/sqrt(T) ) where T is diffusion steps. This work establishes a principled framework for integrating heterogeneous protein representations through learnable diffusion.

papers.title: Relative representations enable zero-shot latent space communication
papers.research_question: Given two different learning models trained separately on different data, can we compare their latent embeddings? The paper investigates how to achieve invariance in latent spaces to enable communication between them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces relative representations, which encode data points by their similarity to a fixed set of anchors. This representation is invariant to angle-preserving transformations in the latent space, enabling zero-shot model stitching and comparison of latent spaces across different trainings, architectures, and data modalities.
papers.conclusion: Relative representations provide a practical and effective way to achieve invariance in latent spaces, enabling zero-shot communication between neural network components and facilitating latent space comparison across diverse settings.
papers.key_findings:
Relative representations preserve the angles between embeddings across different models and training runs, making latent spaces comparable.
The similarity between relative representations of two latent spaces is a strong proxy for model performance, correlating with metrics like accuracy.
Models can be trained end-to-end using relative representations without significant performance drops compared to absolute representations.
Zero-shot stitching of encoder and decoder components from different models (e.g., trained with different seeds, architectures, or on different datasets) is possible using relative representations.
Relative representations enable cross-lingual and cross-architecture zero-shot transfer for tasks like text classification and image reconstruction.
future_direction: Exploring other similarity functions to enforce invariances to non-isometric deformations.
Investigating the use of vector quantization algorithms to achieve invariance to bounded distortion.
papers.abstract: Neural networks embed the geometric structure of a data manifold lying in a high-dimensional space into latent representations. Ideally, the distribution of the data points in the latent space should depend only on the task, the data, the loss, and other architecture-specific constraints. However, factors such as the random weights initialization, training hyperparameters, or other sources of randomness in the training phase may induce incoherent latent spaces that hinder any form of reuse. Nevertheless, we empirically observe that, under the same data and modeling choices, the angles between the encodings within distinct latent spaces do not change. In this work, we propose the latent similarity between each sample and a fixed set of anchors as an alternative data representation, demonstrating that it can enforce the desired invariances without any additional training. We show how neural architectures can leverage these relative representations to guarantee, in practice, invariance to latent isometries and rescalings, effectively enabling latent space communication: from zero-shot model stitching to latent space comparison between diverse settings. We extensively validate the generalization capability of our approach on different datasets, spanning various modalities (images, text, graphs), tasks (e.g., classification, reconstruction) and architectures (e.g., CNNs, GCNs, transformers).

papers.title: Position: Mechanistic Interpretability Should Prioritize Feature Consistency in SAEs
papers.research_question: How can feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be achieved and measured to improve the reliability of mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and proposes the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to measure consistency. It shows that high consistency is achievable with appropriate architectural choices (e.g., TopK SAEs) and that high PW-MCC correlates with semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.conclusion: The paper calls for a community-wide shift towards valuing and systematically measuring feature consistency in SAEs for cumulative progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
High feature consistency (PW-MCC ≈ 0.80) is achievable with TopK SAEs on real-world LLM activations.
PW-MCC reliably tracks ground-truth feature recovery (GT-MCC) in synthetic experiments.
Feature consistency is frequency-dependent: more frequent features are learned more consistently.
Different SAE architectures yield different levels of consistency, with TopK SAEs performing best.
High PW-MCC scores correlate strongly with the semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.limitation:
The focus is on SAEs, and other interpretability methods may have different consistency challenges.
The study uses a specific metric (PW-MCC) for a specific notion of consistency (strong feature consistency).
The real-world experiments are limited to two base models and one dataset.
The automated interpretation pipeline has its own limitations.
future_direction: Extending consistency analysis to other interpretability methods beyond SAEs.
Developing more nuanced metrics for consistency that go beyond strong feature consistency.
Investigating the relationship between consistency and downstream task performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a prominent tool in mechanistic interpretability (MI) for decomposing neural network activations into interpretable features. However, the aspiration to identify a canonical set of features is challenged by the observed inconsistency of learned SAE features across different training runs, undermining the reliability and efficiency of MI research. This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in SAEs -- the reliable convergence to equivalent feature sets across independent runs. We propose using the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to operationalize consistency and demonstrate that high levels are achievable (0.80 for TopK SAEs on LLM activations) with appropriate architectural choices. Our contributions include detailing the benefits of prioritizing consistency; providing theoretical grounding and synthetic validation using a model organism, which verifies PW-MCC as a reliable proxy for ground-truth recovery; and extending these findings to real-world LLM data, where high feature consistency strongly correlates with the semantic similarity of learned feature explanations. We call for a community-wide shift towards systematically measuring feature consistency to foster robust cumulative progress in MI.

papers.title: Analysis of a convolutional neural network for predicting unsteady volume wake flow fields
papers.research_question: How does a convolutional neural network system learn and predict three-dimensional unsteady wake flow dynamics in different flow regimes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a multi-scale CNN system for predicting 3D unsteady wake flow and investigates its mechanisms, showing that convolution layers integrate and transport wavenumber information to extract flow structures, and that redundant feature maps can be identified and removed to reduce model size without loss of performance.
papers.conclusion: The CNN system predicts wake flow by integrating and transporting wavenumber information through convolution layers, extracting representations of flow dynamics. Redundant feature maps can be removed based on structural similarity, significantly reducing model size without performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN system predicts flow in different regimes by transporting wavenumber information through convolution layers.
Feature maps extract similar flow structures (e.g., braid shear layers and shedding vortices) across different Reynolds numbers.
Convolution layers integrate information from all input flow variables and histories, with more recent histories having larger contributions.
Redundant feature maps can be identified using structural similarity (SSIM) and removed, reducing the number of weights by 85% without affecting prediction performance.
papers.abstract: A predictive convolutional neural network is developed to predict the future of three-dimensional unsteady wake flow from past information of flow velocity and pressure. The developed network is found to be capable of predicting vortex dynamics at distinctive flow regimes with flow structures at different scales. Mechanisms of the network on predicting vortex dynamics at two distinctive flow regimes, the mode-B shedding regime and the turbulent wake regime, are investigated. Information in feature maps of the network is visualized and quantitatively assessed to investigate the encoded flow structures. A Fourier analysis is conducted to investigate the mechanisms of the network on learning fluid motions with distinctive flow scales. The transformation of information from the input to prediction layers of the network is tracked to examine how the network transforms the input information for prediction. Structural similarities among feature maps in the network are evaluated to reduce the number of feature maps containing redundant flow structures, which allows reduction of the size of the network without affecting prediction performance.

papers.title: PCAAE: Principal Component Analysis Autoencoder for organising the latent space of generative networks
papers.research_question: How to create an autoencoder with a latent space where components are ordered by decreasing importance and are statistically independent, and how to use this to organize the latent space of pre-trained GANs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Principal Component Analysis Autoencoder (PCAAE), an autoencoder whose latent space has dimensions ordered by decreasing importance and statistically independent components, and shows how to use it to organize the latent space of pre-trained GANs.
papers.conclusion: The PCAAE autoencoder organizes the latent space with decreasing importance and independent components, and can be applied to pre-trained GANs to disentangle their latent spaces, enabling better interpretation and manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
PCAAE creates a latent space where each component corresponds to a distinct attribute of the data, as shown on synthetic ellipses.
PCAAE applied to a pre-trained GAN (PGAN) can disentangle high-level attributes like hair color, head pose, and gender in face images without labels.
The absolute Pearson correlation coefficient shows that PCAAE components are strongly correlated with only one attribute, unlike other methods.
The progressive training and covariance loss effectively organize the latent space in decreasing importance and independence.
PCAAE can be applied to any pre-trained generative model to organize its latent space post-hoc.
papers.limitation:
Increasing the latent space size by one at each step can be problematic where the autoencoder needs more freedom.
The use of ℓ2 norm reconstruction loss may not be optimal for complex data like CelebA, leading to blurry results.
A PCAAE trained in one region of a GAN latent space is not necessarily valid for another region.
future_direction: Increase the latent space by small packets of codes instead of one at a time.
Replace the ℓ2 norm reconstruction loss with a perceptual metric for better results on complex data.
Create a PCAAE that is applicable to the whole latent space of a GAN.
papers.abstract: Autoencoders and generative models produce some of the most spectacular deep learning results to date. However, understanding and controlling the latent space of these models presents a considerable challenge. Drawing inspiration from principal component analysis and autoencoder, we propose the Principal Component Analysis Autoencoder (PCAAE). This is a novel autoencoder whose latent space verifies two properties. Firstly, the dimensions are organised in decreasing importance with respect to the data at hand. Secondly, the components of the latent space are statistically independent. We achieve this by progressively increasing the latent space during training, and with a covariance loss applied to the latent codes. The resulting autoencoder produces a latent space which separates the intrinsic attributes of the data into different components of the latent space, in a completely unsupervised manner. We also describe an extension of our approach to the case of powerful, pre-trained GANs. We show results on both synthetic examples of shapes and on a state-of-the-art GAN. For example, we are able to separate the color shade scale of hair and skin, pose of faces and the gender in the CelebA, without accessing any labels. We compare the PCAAE with other state-of-the-art approaches, in particular with respect to the ability to disentangle attributes in the latent space. We hope that this approach will contribute to better understanding of the intrinsic latent spaces of powerful deep generative models.

papers.title: Video Prediction of Dynamic Physical Simulations With Pixel-Space Spatiotemporal Transformers
papers.research_question: This study investigates a transformer adaptation for video prediction with a simple end-to-end approach, comparing various spatiotemporal self-attention layouts, focusing on causal modelling of physical simulations over time.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a simple, interpretable pure transformer model (PSViT) for end-to-end autoregressive video prediction in pixel-space, which extends the time horizon for physically accurate predictions by up to 50% compared to existing latent-space approaches.
papers.conclusion: The presented simple, interpretable pure transformer for end-to-end autoregressive video prediction extends the horizon for physically accurate predictions while maintaining competitive performance on standard video quality metrics, highlighting the benefits of a straightforward end-to-end approach.
papers.key_findings:
The PSViT model achieves increased temporal accuracy in predicting PDE-driven video sequences compared to existing approaches, as measured by an object tracking metric.
The model maintains competitive performance on standard video quality metrics (SSIM, PSNR).
Interpretability experiments identify network regions that encode information useful for estimating PDE simulation parameters via probing.
The learned encoding of underlying physics generalizes to the estimation of out-of-distribution simulation parameters.
The model's performance is evaluated on several physics simulation datasets and common video prediction benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
For three of the simulation datasets increasing PSViT model size has minimal impact on performance over time.
For stochastic video-generation results on BAIR, the approach falls short compared to latent space models.
Object shapes, although positioned accurately, can distort over time, particularly when rotation is involved.
By performing end-to-end training, the model doesn't benefit from the large-scale pretrained image encoders/decoders often employed by latent space models.
future_direction: Developing more sophisticated metrics for evaluating physical accuracy, moving beyond current object-based pixel distance methods.
Training larger models on higher-resolution datasets featuring increased visual fidelity and physical complexity.
papers.abstract: Inspired by the performance and scalability of autoregressive large language models (LLMs), transformer-based models have seen recent success in the visual domain. This study investigates a transformer adaptation for video prediction with a simple end-to-end approach, comparing various spatiotemporal self-attention layouts. Focusing on causal modeling of physical simulations over time; a common shortcoming of existing video-generative approaches, we attempt to isolate spatiotemporal reasoning via physical object tracking metrics and unsupervised training on physical simulation datasets. We introduce a simple yet effective pure transformer model for autoregressive video prediction, utilizing continuous pixel-space representations for video prediction. Without the need for complex training strategies or latent feature-learning components, our approach significantly extends the time horizon for physically accurate predictions by up to 50% when compared with existing latent-space approaches, while maintaining comparable performance on common video quality metrics. In addition, we conduct interpretability experiments to identify network regions that encode information useful to perform accurate estimations of PDE simulation parameters via probing models, and find that this generalizes to the estimation of out-of-distribution simulation parameters. This work serves as a platform for further attention-based spatiotemporal modeling of videos via a simple, parameter efficient, and interpretable approach.

papers.title: It's FLAN time! Summing feature-wise latent representations for\n interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we build deep learning models that are both powerful and interpretable by constraining the architecture to process features separately and sum their latent representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FLANs, a class of structurally-constrained neural networks that are interpretable by design, achieving good performance on various benchmarks while allowing for native interpretability without post-hoc methods.
papers.conclusion: FLANs represent a powerful and interpretable model class that can be easily and natively interpreted without the need for post-hoc methods, making them suitable for high-stakes applications.
papers.key_findings:
FLANs achieve performance comparable to established models on a series of benchmark datasets across tabular, image, and text domains.
FLANs can be interpreted via three modalities: separating and predicting the effect of individual features, feature importance via latent representation norms, and example-based explanations via nearest neighbors in the latent space.
Quantitative evaluation using interpretability metrics shows that FLANs' native interpretability is on par with post-hoc feature attribution methods.
FLANs can achieve 100% training accuracy, indicating the ability to learn complex interactions, but may generalize less well on some complex datasets like CUB-200-2011 and IMDb.
The structural constraints of FLANs (feature-wise processing and summation) facilitate interpretability without excessively compromising test performance.
papers.limitation:
FLANs may have difficulties learning complex/long interactions, as evidenced by lower performance on the IMDb and CUB-200-2011 datasets.
The non-sensitivity metric indicates FLANs may assign importance to non-influential features or no importance to influential features, especially in patch-based image classification where attribution scores are averaged over patches.
future_direction: Address the generalization difficulties of the model.
Run user studies to further validate the interpretability of the model.
papers.abstract:
Interpretability has become a necessary feature for machine learning models
deployed in critical scenarios, e.g. legal system, healthcare. In these
situations, algorithmic decisions may have (potentially negative) long-lasting
effects on the end-user affected by the decision. In many cases, the
representational power of deep learning models is not needed, therefore simple
and interpretable models (e.g. linear models) should be preferred. However, in
high-dimensional and/or complex domains (e.g. computer vision), the universal
approximation capabilities of neural networks are required. Inspired by linear
models and the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, we propose a novel
class of structurally-constrained neural networks, which we call FLANs
(Feature-wise Latent Additive Networks). Crucially, FLANs process each input
feature separately, computing for each of them a representation in a common
latent space. These feature-wise latent representations are then simply summed,
and the aggregated representation is used for prediction. These constraints
(which are at the core of the interpretability of linear models) allow a user
to estimate the effect of each individual feature independently from the
others, enhancing interpretability. In a set of experiments across different
domains, we show how without compromising excessively the test performance, the
structural constraints proposed in FLANs indeed facilitates the
interpretability of deep learning models. We quantitatively compare FLANs
interpretability to post-hoc methods using recently introduced metrics,
discussing the advantages of natively interpretable models over a post-hoc
analysis.

papers.title: Explainability Techniques for Chemical Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we explain the predictions of chemical language models by attributing importance to individual atoms in the input molecular string?
papers.core_contribution: We propose an explainable AI technique for chemical language models that attributes the importance of individual atoms to the model's predictions by backpropagating relevance through attention scores and gradients, and visualize the importance on the molecular structure.
papers.conclusion: We propose an attribution technique for Transformers operating on molecular string representations, which provides interpretable predictions and allows inspection of the model's learned features for solubility prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method achieves competitive predictive performance on aqueous and organic solvent solubility prediction tasks.
The visualizations highlight atoms that are important for solubility, which can be validated by chemists.
The model sometimes attributes high relevance to the carbon backbone, which may be due to the pretraining procedure.
The method is applicable to self-attention Transformers and can be extended to other architectures.
papers.limitation:
The method only visualizes atom tokens and does not handle non-atom tokens (e.g., bonds, brackets) in the SMILES string.
The model does not enforce invariance to different SMILES representations of the same molecule.
future_direction: Extend the visualization to non-atom tokens in the SMILES string.
Enforce SMILES invariance in the model through contrastive training.
Apply the explainability technique to other Transformer architectures, such as generative models.
papers.abstract: Explainability techniques are crucial in gaining insights into the reasons behind the predictions of deep learning models, which have not yet been applied to chemical language models. We propose an explainable AI technique that attributes the importance of individual atoms towards the predictions made by these models. Our method backpropagates the relevance information towards the chemical input string and visualizes the importance of individual atoms. We focus on self-attention Transformers operating on molecular string representations and leverage a pretrained encoder for finetuning. We showcase the method by predicting and visualizing solubility in water and organic solvents. We achieve competitive model performance while obtaining interpretable predictions, which we use to inspect the pretrained model.

papers.title: Transformers and the representation of biomedical background knowledge
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether transformer-based models encode biomedical domain knowledge at entity and relational levels, how they handle complex facts, differences between models, and their response to evidence biases in the literature.
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that transformer-based models encode biomedical knowledge, but fine-tuning can lose some semantic structure, and it highlights risks of misclassification due to dataset biases.
papers.conclusion: Transformers encode biomedical knowledge useful for inference, but careful evaluation is needed due to biases and information loss during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers like BioBERT and BioMegatron encode biomedical domain knowledge at entity and relational levels.
Fine-tuning for specific tasks can lead to loss of semantic information about entity types.
Clustering analysis shows that representations form biologically meaningful groups, such as genes from the same pathways.
Classification errors are correlated with the frequency of entities in the training data, indicating bias.
Despite strong evidence, some well-known clinical relations can be misclassified by the models.
papers.limitation: Models may misclassify well-known clinical relations due to biases in the dataset.
papers.abstract: Specialised transformers-based models (such as BioBERT and BioMegatron) are adapted for the biomedical domain based on publicly available biomedical corpora. As such, they have the potential to encode large-scale biological knowledge. We investigate the encoding and representation of biological knowledge in these models, and its potential utility to support inference in cancer precision medicine - namely, the interpretation of the clinical significance of genomic alterations. We compare the performance of different transformer baselines; we use probing to determine the consistency of encodings for distinct entities; and we use clustering methods to compare and contrast the internal properties of the embeddings for genes, variants, drugs and diseases. We show that these models do indeed encode biological knowledge, although some of this is lost in fine-tuning for specific tasks. Finally, we analyse how the models behave with regard to biases and imbalances in the dataset.

papers.title: Learning local discrete features in explainable-by-design convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we design a convolutional neural network that is both high-performance and explainable by using a lateral inhibition mechanism to learn local discrete features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ExplaiNet, an explainable-by-design CNN that uses a lateral inhibition layer to learn local discrete feature vectors, enabling high accuracy and providing explanations via a probabilistic graph and motif discovery.
papers.conclusion: The ExplaiNet framework breaks the performance-explainability trade-off by introducing an explainable-by-design CNN that retains or surpasses baseline performance while providing causal explanations based on discrete feature motifs.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed ExplaiNet model achieves comparable or better performance than baseline ResNet and DenseNet architectures on tiny image datasets while providing explanations.
The lateral inhibition layer amplifies gradients of winner neurons, leading to ordered activations and the formation of local discrete feature vectors.
Feature motif discovery using the EXTREME algorithm reduces the vocabulary of local discrete features, providing concise explanations.
The explainer probabilistic graph can infer causal relationships between motifs of adjacent levels and attribute the model's output to global motifs.
Experiments show that the explainer can sometimes correctly classify samples that the neural predictor misclassifies, suggesting potential for ensemble use or adversarial sample detection.
papers.limitation:
Further research on regularization aspects of the lateral inhibition function is required to investigate the magnitude of weights and activations during training.
Experiments are limited to tiny image datasets due to computational resources; the method has not been tested on medium-resolution images or high numbers of classes.
future_direction: Investigate the proper amount of weight decay and restriction of input values for positively monotonic gradient amplification in the lateral inhibition function.
Scale up the method to train models on medium-resolution images, high number of classes, and with millions of parameters.
Adjust the EXTREME algorithm to support custom numeric system bases, making the conversion to the quaternary system optional.
papers.abstract: Our proposed framework attempts to break the trade-off between performance and explainability by introducing an explainable-by-design convolutional neural network (CNN) based on the lateral inhibition mechanism. The ExplaiNet model consists of the predictor, that is a high-accuracy CNN with residual or dense skip connections, and the explainer probabilistic graph that expresses the spatial interactions of the network neurons. The value on each graph node is a local discrete feature (LDF) vector, a patch descriptor that represents the indices of antagonistic neurons ordered by the strength of their activations, which are learned with gradient descent. Using LDFs as sequences we can increase the conciseness of explanations by repurposing EXTREME, an EM-based sequence motif discovery method that is typically used in molecular biology. Having a discrete feature motif matrix for each one of intermediate image representations, instead of a continuous activation tensor, allows us to leverage the inherent explainability of Bayesian networks. By collecting observations and directly calculating probabilities, we can explain causal relationships between motifs of adjacent levels and attribute the model's output to global motifs. Moreover, experiments on various tiny image benchmark datasets confirm that our predictor ensures the same level of performance as the baseline architecture for a given count of parameters and/or layers. Our novel method shows promise to exceed this performance while providing an additional stream of explanations. In the solved MNIST classification task, it reaches a comparable to the state-of-the-art performance for single models, using standard training setup and 0.75 million parameters.

papers.title: Explaining reaction coordinates of alanine dipeptide isomerization obtained from deep neural networks using Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)
papers.research_question: How can Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods explain which collective variables contribute to the reaction coordinates predicted by deep neural networks for alanine dipeptide isomerization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that XAI methods (LIME and SHAP) can provide local explanations for the contribution of collective variables to reaction coordinates predicted by a deep neural network for alanine dipeptide isomerization, revealing the importance of specific dihedral angles.
papers.conclusion: The proposed AI-aided method combined with XAI provides a practical tool for locally explaining appropriate reaction coordinates from DNN training, especially near the transition state, and is applicable to complex molecular systems.
papers.key_findings:
Deep neural networks can be trained to predict appropriate reaction coordinates for alanine dipeptide isomerization.
Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanation (LIME) and Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) provide local explanations of feature contributions to the predicted reaction coordinates.
Near the transition state, the dihedral angle θ becomes more important than near the stable states, indicating its role in crossing the barrier.
The feature contributions from LIME and SHAP are consistent, justifying LIME's linear model assumption.
The method can identify dominant collective variables consistent with previous committor test analyses.
papers.limitation: Understanding the detailed mechanism for complex molecular systems becomes complicated because of the large numbers of collective variables.
future_direction: Application to solute-solvent systems such as alanine dipeptide in explicit water.
Application to various other solute-solvent systems.
papers.abstract: A method for obtaining appropriate reaction coordinates is required to identify transition states distinguishing the product and reactant in complex molecular systems. Recently, abundant research has been devoted to obtaining reaction coordinates using artificial neural networks from deep learning literature, where many collective variables are typically utilized in the input layer. However, it is difficult to explain the details of which collective variables contribute to the predicted reaction coordinates owing to the complexity of the nonlinear functions in deep neural networks. To overcome this limitation, we used Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods of the Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanation (LIME) and the game theory-based framework known as Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). We demonstrated that XAI enables us to obtain the degree of contribution of each collective variable to reaction coordinates that is determined by nonlinear regressions with deep learning for the committor of the alanine dipeptide isomerization in vacuum. In particular, both LIME and SHAP provide important features to the predicted reaction coordinates, which are characterized by appropriate dihedral angles consistent with those previously reported from the committor test analysis. The present study offers an AI-aided framework to explain the appropriate reaction coordinates, which acquires considerable significance when the number of degrees of freedom increases.

papers.title: Human in the Latent Loop (HILL): Interactively Guiding Model Training Through Human Intuition
papers.research_question: How can human intuition be incorporated into model training via interactive latent space modifications to improve model performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces HILL, an interactive framework that allows users to incorporate human intuition into model training by reshaping latent space representations, using a knowledge distillation-inspired loss to integrate user modifications.
papers.conclusion: HILL facilitates a novel human-AI interaction paradigm that improves model performance and convergence while maintaining generalization, bridging the gap between data-driven optimization and human-centric understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Human-guided latent space modifications enhance model performance and convergence while maintaining generalization.
Participants employed diverse strategies such as increasing cluster compactness and maximizing class separation.
The approach demonstrates robustness, with even the worst-performing HILL runs outperforming the baseline.
Human intuition can highlight relevant decision boundaries that standard optimization fails to capture.
There are risks of including user biases and preconceived notions into the model.
papers.limitation:
Users bring their own preconceived notions which can subtly shape their engagement and the resulting model behavior, potentially reinforcing subjective structures.
Some participants struggled to gauge whether their interactions were meaningful, indicating a need for more transparent algorithmic feedback.
future_direction: Explore adaptive strategies where the model learns which human interventions are beneficial and adjusts its reliance accordingly.
Develop more explicit feedback mechanisms beyond pure performance metrics, such as visualizing differences between latent spaces before and after intervention.
papers.abstract: Latent space representations are critical for understanding and improving the behavior of machine learning models, yet they often remain obscure and intricate. Understanding and exploring the latent space has the potential to contribute valuable human intuition and expertise about respective domains. In this work, we present HILL, an interactive framework allowing users to incorporate human intuition into the model training by interactively reshaping latent space representations. The modifications are infused into the model training loop via a novel approach inspired by knowledge distillation, treating the user's modifications as a teacher to guide the model in reshaping its intrinsic latent representation. The process allows the model to converge more effectively and overcome inefficiencies, as well as provide beneficial insights to the user. We evaluated HILL in a user study tasking participants to train an optimal model, closely observing the employed strategies. The results demonstrated that human-guided latent space modifications enhance model performance while maintaining generalization, yet also revealing the risks of including user biases. Our work introduces a novel human-AI interaction paradigm that infuses human intuition into model training and critically examines the impact of human intervention on training strategies and potential biases.

papers.title: Learned feature representations are biased by complexity, learning order, position, and more
papers.research_question: How do extraneous properties like feature complexity, learning order, and distribution affect the learned feature representations in deep neural networks, even when features play equivalent computational roles?
papers.core_contribution: Learned feature representations in deep networks are systematically biased by extraneous properties like feature complexity and learning order, which poses significant challenges for interpretability and comparing representations across systems.
papers.conclusion: The systematic biases in learned feature representations highlight a key challenge for interpretability and for comparing representations between models and brains, as extraneous learning details can be conflated with computationally important aspects.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler features are represented more strongly and densely than complex features, even when both are learned equally well.
Features learned earlier dominate representations, making them path-dependent.
Feature prevalence in the training data and output position also bias representation strength.
These biases are general across architectures (MLPs, ResNets, Transformers) but can interact with hyperparameters like dropout and optimizer.
These representation biases impact downstream analyses like interpretability methods and Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA).
papers.limitation:
Focus on simple, synthetic datasets.
Focus on classification tasks; continuous functions or richer contextual computation (e.g., language modeling) may differ.
Models are of toy scale; biases may differ in larger models.
Main analyses rely on linear regression, which may miss non-linear encodings.
future_direction: Study these biases on more realistic datasets with larger sets of entangled features.
Investigate how biases differ under other objectives (e.g., continuous functions) and in richly contextual computation.
Explore these effects at scale in larger models.
papers.abstract: Representation learning, and interpreting learned representations, are key areas of focus in machine learning and neuroscience. Both fields generally use representations as a means to understand or improve a system's computations. In this work, however, we explore surprising dissociations between representation and computation that may pose challenges for such efforts. We create datasets in which we attempt to match the computational role that different features play, while manipulating other properties of the features or the data. We train various deep learning architectures to compute these multiple abstract features about their inputs. We find that their learned feature representations are systematically biased towards representing some features more strongly than others, depending upon extraneous properties such as feature complexity, the order in which features are learned, and the distribution of features over the inputs. For example, features that are simpler to compute or learned first tend to be represented more strongly and densely than features that are more complex or learned later, even if all features are learned equally well. We also explore how these biases are affected by architectures, optimizers, and training regimes (e.g., in transformers, features decoded earlier in the output sequence also tend to be represented more strongly). Our results help to characterize the inductive biases of gradient-based representation learning. We then illustrate the downstream effects of these biases on various commonly-used methods for analyzing or intervening on representations. These results highlight a key challenge for interpretability $-$ or for comparing the representations of models and brains $-$ disentangling extraneous biases from the computationally important aspects of a system's internal representations.

papers.title: Latent Thinking Optimization: Your Latent Reasoning Language Model Secretly Encodes Reward Signals in Its Latent Thoughts
papers.research_question: Do latent thoughts that lead to correct answers exhibit different patterns in latent space compared to those leading to incorrect answers?
papers.core_contribution: Latent thoughts in reasoning models encode reward signals predictive of answer correctness, enabling a Latent Thinking Optimization (LTO) algorithm that uses a Latent Reward Model (LRM) to sample better latent thinking trajectories and improve reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: The research demonstrates that latent thoughts encode reward signals, enabling efficient reward modeling and optimization directly in the latent space via LTO, which improves reasoning performance across diverse tasks and models, highlighting a promising direction for scalable and efficient LLM thinking.
papers.key_findings:
Latent thoughts leading to correct vs. incorrect answers exhibit distinct patterns in latent space, with correct thoughts having richer information, less noise, and more structured geometries.
A lightweight latent classifier (LRM) can reliably predict answer correctness directly from latent thought trajectories, even from partial sequences.
The Latent Thinking Optimization (LTO) algorithm, which uses the LRM to weight and sample latent trajectories, significantly improves reasoning accuracy across diverse tasks and models.
The latent reward signals and LTO method generalize across domains and can be applied to general LLMs by interpreting their hidden states as latent thoughts.
Reward modeling and test-time compute scaling can be performed efficiently in the latent space, offering a domain-agnostic alternative to natural language-based methods.
papers.limitation:
LTO optimizes by selectively sampling correct trajectories rather than directly modifying the base model's thinking policy; it cannot improve performance if the base model's policy is too poor (e.g., generates only incorrect thoughts).
The reward signals are binary (correct/incorrect) and do not capture other dimensions like safety or helpfulness, limiting multi-objective optimization.
future_direction: Integrate latent reward signals into a reinforcement learning-based preference optimization framework to directly optimize the latent thinking policy.
Extend the latent classifier to incorporate multiple reward dimensions (e.g., safety, helpfulness) for multi-objective latent thinking optimization.
Design adaptive mechanisms to identify the optimal number of thinking steps to balance base model performance and trajectory diversity for LTO.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at problem solving by generating chain of thoughts in natural language, but such verbal thinking is computationally costly and prone to overthinking. Recent work instead proposes a latent thinking architecture Huginn-3.5B, which represents intermediate reasoning steps as sequence of latent representations. However, latent thoughts lack interpretability and are difficult to supervise, raising concerns about the correctness and reliability of its latent thinking processes. In this paper, we provide a systematic study of how Huginn-3.5B thinks in the latent space and how external supervision signals can improve its latent thinking processes. We show that latent thoughts leading to correct versus incorrect answers exhibit highly distinguishable patterns, and that a latent classifier can reliably predict answer correctness directly from latent thoughts. Leveraging these insights, we propose Latent Thinking Optimization (LTO), a probabilistic algorithm that employs the latent classifier as a Latent Reward Model (LRM) to optimize the latent thinking processes. Extensive experiments across diverse reasoning tasks demonstrate that LRM is highly effective in detecting incorrect latent thinking patterns, and LTO can significantly improve the latent thinking processes. Furthermore, we show that LRM can generalize across diverse domains, and LTO can be seamlessly applied to general LLMs to improve their thinking processes. In contrast to verbal thinking, our method demonstrates that reward modeling and scaling test-time thinking with supervision can be performed directly in the latent space, highlighting its potential as a general, efficient, and domain-agnostic approach to improving the thinking processes of LLMs.

papers.title: Interpreting the Latent Space of GANs for Semantic Face Editing
papers.research_question: How are semantic attributes encoded in the latent space of GANs, and how can this understanding be used for semantic face editing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes InterFaceGAN, a framework that interprets the latent semantics learned by GANs and demonstrates that linear subspaces in the latent space correspond to specific facial attributes, enabling precise semantic editing without retraining the model.
papers.conclusion: GANs spontaneously learn disentangled and controllable facial attribute representations in their latent space, and the InterFaceGAN framework can effectively interpret and manipulate these semantics for both synthetic and real image editing.
papers.key_findings:
Linear hyperplanes in the latent space of well-trained GANs can separate binary facial attributes with high accuracy.
Moving a latent code along the normal direction of a semantic hyperplane allows for continuous control of that attribute in the generated image.
Attributes like age, gender, and eyeglasses are entangled in the latent space, but can be decoupled via subspace projection for independent manipulation.
The style-based generator of StyleGAN learns a more disentangled latent representation (W space) compared to the traditional latent space (Z space).
The interpreted semantics can be applied to edit real face images by first inverting them into the GAN's latent space.
papers.limitation:
Moving the latent code too far from the semantic boundary causes severe changes in appearance, making the edited image no longer resemble the original person.
Inverting real images to the latent space of pre-trained GANs is non-trivial and current inversion methods show poor performance for some models, leading to reconstruction discrepancies.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent advance of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) in high-fidelity image synthesis, there lacks enough understanding of how GANs are able to map a latent code sampled from a random distribution to a photo-realistic image. Previous work assumes the latent space learned by GANs follows a distributed representation but observes the vector arithmetic phenomenon. In this work, we propose a novel framework, called InterFaceGAN, for semantic face editing by interpreting the latent semantics learned by GANs. In this framework, we conduct a detailed study on how different semantics are encoded in the latent space of GANs for face synthesis. We find that the latent code of well-trained generative models actually learns a disentangled representation after linear transformations. We explore the disentanglement between various semantics and manage to decouple some entangled semantics with subspace projection, leading to more precise control of facial attributes. Besides manipulating gender, age, expression, and the presence of eyeglasses, we can even vary the face pose as well as fix the artifacts accidentally generated by GAN models. The proposed method is further applied to achieve real image manipulation when combined with GAN inversion methods or some encoder-involved models. Extensive results suggest that learning to synthesize faces spontaneously brings a disentangled and controllable facial attribute representation.

papers.title: Behavior and Representation in Large Language Models for Combinatorial Optimization: From Feature Extraction to Algorithm Selection
papers.research_question: To what extent do LLMs capture information about combinatorial optimization problems, and can their internal representations support downstream tasks like algorithm selection?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can implicitly encode meaningful structural information about combinatorial optimization problems in their hidden layers, and these representations are comparable to handcrafted features for the task of per-instance algorithm selection.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can serve as general-purpose feature extractors for combinatorial optimization problems, capturing structural information relevant to algorithmic performance and supporting tasks like algorithm selection.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can reliably infer simple instance features directly from textual representations, but struggle with features requiring computation.
Natural language representations yield the best performance in direct querying, followed by code-like, with standard formats performing worst.
Probing hidden layers can recover complex features better than direct querying, especially for high-computation features.
LLM-derived representations are effective for per-instance algorithm selection, achieving performance comparable to traditional handcrafted features.
The choice of pooling strategy (mean, max, last) and classifier (LightGBM, Logistic Regression, MLP) affects algorithm selection accuracy.
papers.limitation: LLMs exhibit limited numerical and procedural reasoning capabilities, struggling to infer features that require even minimal computation.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex problems and representations.
Investigating the effect of model size and architecture on representation quality.
Exploring the use of LLM representations for other optimization tasks, such as performance prediction.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have opened new perspectives for automation in optimization. While several studies have explored how LLMs can generate or solve optimization models, far less is understood about what these models actually learn regarding problem structure or algorithmic behavior. This study investigates how LLMs internally represent combinatorial optimization problems and whether such representations can support downstream decision tasks.
